entry.title: Natural Language (NL) Over SAP Data: A Practical MCP Pattern for Joule Desktop & Pro-Code Agent
entry.content:
Introduction

Any S/4HANA OData API, standard or custom, can be exposed as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway and consumed by AI agents through two complementary paths: Joule Work Desktop for a direct, low-overhead experience, and a custom agent in Cloud Foundry that can be triggered in Joule SAP Build Work Zone for an orchestrated, reasoning-capable experience. 

To make it concrete, we applied it to SAP Production Revenue Accounting (PRA) data: a domain that is rich, complex, and mission-critical, and where the gap between the data and the people who need it is wide enough to make the pattern's value immediately visible. The solution is not PRA-specific. The same architecture applies to any standard or custom OData V4 service in S/4HANA: Finance, Plant Maintenance, Materials Management, Sales and Distribution, or any domain where business users need structured answers without writing queries or navigating transaction codes.

This blog walks through the architecture, the components, the implementation decisions, and the trade-offs behind the two access patterns we designed and deployed:

  1. Joule Work Desktop — connects directly to an custom MCP server published via SAP Integration Suite. Ideal for business users who want a direct AI interface to standard PRA revenue accounting tables.

  2. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone — routes through a custom AI agent on SAP Cloud Foundry that adds an intelligent reasoning layer. Ideal for business users already operating inside Work Zone.

Both patterns share the same backend: a custom OData V4 service exposing standard SAP PRA tables, published as an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway.

A full end-to-end walkthrough has been recorded as a companion to this blog.

Solution Architecture

The architecture is deliberately generic. Swap out the PRA OData service for any other S/4HANA OData V4 endpoint and the rest of the pattern holds unchanged.

The solution exposes standard S/4HANA PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service (built on ABAP RAP), publishes them as governed MCP tools through SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway, and surfaces them to business users via natural language either directly through Joule Work Desktop or through a custom AI agent embedded in SAP Build Work Zone.

Path 1 — Joule Desktop:

Desktop User → Joule Desktop → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Path 2 — Joule in Work Zone:

Web User → SAP Build Work Zone (Joule) → A2A → Custom Agent on CF → MCP → SAP Integration Suite → OData → S/4HANA

Component Walkthrough

1. S/4HANA On-Premise — The Data Source

The data lives in a standard S/4HANA on-premise system. We exposed the standard PRA tables via a custom OData V4 service built using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

The service exposes all 13 entity sets with proper navigation associations, enabling deep $expand queries across both the Document and Revenue Distribution branches. 

 

2. SAP Integration Suite — MCP Gateway

This is the integration layer that bridges the RAP OData service into the AI world.

SAP Integration Suite's MCP Server capability (part of the MCP Gateway feature, available with the Premium subscription) consumes the OData V4 service metadata and automatically generates MCP tool definitions for every operation. For our 13-entity service, this produced 41 MCP tools covering list queries, filtered reads, and navigation operations.

Why MCP? The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for AI tool discovery and invocation. By publishing our OData service as an MCP server, we make it consumable by any MCP-compatible client, including Joule Work Desktop, LangChain agents, or any future client, without changing the backend.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

The Developer Hub within Integration Suite is used to publish the MCP server, generating the OAuth credentials that clients use to authenticate. It also provides discoverability within the organization: other developers can find and reuse the same MCP server without rebuilding the integration from scratch.

3. SAP Cloud Foundry — Custom Reasoning Agent

For the Work Zone path, we built a custom Python agent deployed on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry. This agent adds the reasoning layer that bridges Joule's natural language input to structured MCP tool calls.

The agent stack:

ComponentRole

a2a-sdk

Implements the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, exposing a JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint that Joule can call

LangGraph + LangChain

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) loop: decides which MCP tools to call, in what order, based on the user's question

langchain-mcp-adapters

Loads MCP tools from Integration Suite at runtime and wraps them as LangChain 

LiteLLM / langchain-litellm

Routes LLM calls to SAP AI Core using the standard OpenAI-compatible interface

The ReAct pattern is important here. Rather than a single-shot query, the agent reasons iteratively: it reads the question, identifies which MCP tools are relevant, calls them, evaluates the results, and decides whether additional calls are needed before formulating the final answer. This is what makes it capable of answering multi-hop questions that require joining data from multiple PRA tables.

4. Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

Deployment uses the Joule CLI. The deploy command registers the custom agent as a Joule capability. By default, this deploys to standalone Joule.

To surface the agent inside SAP Build Work Zone, update the assistant type to sap_digital_Assistant. The Joule Admin Center (accessible by appending /admin to the Joule instance URL) allows you to verify the deployment and confirm the capability is active.

5. SAP Build Work Zone - Registering the A2A Agent with Joule

SAP Build Work Zone is the standard business user entry point. Joule is embedded natively in the Work Zone shell,  no separate app to open, no separate login.

6. Joule Work Desktop Experience

For users who prefer the Joule Work Desktop standalone experience, the integration is simpler: Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server. No custom agent, no A2A, no Cloud Foundry deployment required.

Conclusion

The architecture supports two distinct experiences from the same foundation. Joule Work Desktop connects directly to the MCP server no agent required giving business users a fast, lightweight path to query SAP data in natural language. Joule in SAP Build Work Zone routes through a custom AI agent deployed on BTP Cloud Foundry, adding multi-step reasoning, tool orchestration, and a governed conversational interface for broader business user adoption.

The architecture is composable by design. The OData V4 service, MCP server, reasoning agent, and Joule capability are independent layers each doing one thing well. Swap the data source and the pattern applies to any SAP domain. Complexity lives where it belongs: the OData layer owns the data model, MCP handles tool discoverability, LangGraph handles reasoning, and Joule handles the conversation.

Consider which of your OData APIs could benefit from this pattern  a Finance posting service, a Plant Maintenance feed, a Sales Order status endpoint. Any of them can become a natural language interface using exactly this stack.

entry.title: Unlock Your KPI Insights Instantly with SAP Joule: Introducing the Smart Business KPI Capability
entry.content:
The Problem Every Business User Knows

Your company tracks dozens of KPIs. They're spread across finance, procurement, and operations — each living inside a different Fiori app, behind a different tile, reached through a different set of clicks. Every morning you navigate the same menus to find the same reports. The data is there. Getting to it is just... slow.

What if you could skip all of that and just ask?

Meet the Smart Business KPI Capability for SAP Joule

The Smart Business KPI (SSB KPI) Capability brings your performance dashboards directly into Joule's conversational interface. Ask a plain-language question — get a clickable, navigable KPI card back, right inside the chat pane.

No new configuration. No new data models. The Smart Business KPI capability connects directly to your existing setup.

See It in Action: An AR Manager's Morning

Take an Accounts Receivable Manager who needs to check Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) and related collection KPIs at the start of each day. Previously: open the Fiori Launchpad, locate the AR overview tile, navigate into the report.

Now they open Joule and type: "Show me my assigned KPIs."

Joule returns a KPI Overview card listing every Smart Business KPI assigned to their role — all 30-something of them. They spot the appropriate KPI immediately, click it, and land directly in the runtime report: live values, threshold indicators, trend charts. No manual effort or searching required, just a natural-language request and the relevant details, instantly ! This is the experience this capability is designed to deliver.

What You Can Ask

"Show me my assigned KPIs" · "List my KPIs" · "What KPIs do I have?"

Joule retrieves all Smart Business KPIs assigned to your user role — regardless of threshold status — and presents them in a KPI Overview card. Each item is a direct deep link: one click opens the KPI's runtime report in the correct Fiori application, with the evaluation context already applied.

Why It Matters

Zero navigation overhead

No need to remember which tile leads to which KPI. Just ask.

Role-relevant results only

You see exactly what you're assigned — nothing more, nothing less.

One click to live data

Every KPI card item deep-links to the runtime report with evaluation context pre-loaded.

Works in 40+ languages

Full localization including Arabic, Hebrew, Japanese, Chinese, and all major European languages.

Secure by design

Data retrieval uses your existing SSO session — users see only what they're already entitled to see.

No extra setup

Connects to your existing Smart Business KPI setup with no new data modeling required.

How It Works

When you ask Joule about your KPIs, it understands your intent, retrieves the relevant Smart Business KPIs using your existing SSO authentication, and formats them into a UI5 Integration Card native to the Joule interface.

Every item in the card carries Intent-Based Navigation (IBN) links — the KPI's Semantic Object, Action, and Evaluation or Report ID are embedded as parameters, so one click opens the exact right Fiori application with the exact right context.

Try it today: Ask Joule "Show me my assigned KPIs" in your SAP S/4HANA Cloud 2612 environment. We'd love to hear how it fits your workflow — share your experience in the comments.

entry.title: The Evolution of the SAP User Interface: From SAP GUI to Fiori to Joule Work
entry.content:
The Evolution of the SAP User Interface: From SAP GUI to Fiori to Joule Work

From transactions to intuitive apps to AI-powered collaboration – the SAP user experience is not just changing its appearance. It is changing the way we work.

Anyone who has worked with SAP for a long time will remember it: the classic SAP GUI, countless transaction codes, complex screens, and a user interface that was primarily designed to do one thing – provide functionality.

But the world has changed. And so have our expectations of enterprise software.

Looking back, we can see just how far we have come – and what this evolution means for us as people.

1. SAP GUI – The Era of Transactions

Throughout the 1990s and well beyond, SAP GUI was the central entry point to business processes in countless companies.

The interface was powerful, stable, and designed to support complex business processes. To use SAP efficiently, users had to become familiar with transaction codes, screens, fields, and process logic.

People had to learn how SAP worked.

Over the years, experienced users developed an enormous amount of knowledge. They knew which transaction to use, which fields mattered, and which steps were required to achieve the desired result.

It worked – but shift began in the design of the user experience.

Instead of complex transaction screens, the focus moved towards role-based apps, modern design, and more intuitive interaction. The user experience became increasingly aligned with people's tasks and needs.

Information was meant to be easier to access. Processes were meant to become more understandable. And SAP was increasingly expected to feel as intuitive as the modern applications we use in everyday life.

The key question changed: Not just “How does this transaction work?” but “What task do I want to accomplish?”

With Fiori, access to SAP became more modern, flexible, and better suited to different roles and devices.

This was more than a new design. It was an important step towards a better user experience and a stronger focus on people.

3. Joule Work – From Using Software to AI-Powered Collaboration

With generative AI, the next chapter of the SAP user experience is beginning.

AI assistants such as Joule make it possible to ask for information in natural language, understand relationships more quickly, and receive intelligent support when completing certain tasks.

With Joule Work, SAP is taking this approach further towards an AI-powered work environment. The aim is to bring information and work contexts together more effectively and support tasks across different applications and business processes.

Instead of navigating exclusively through menus and applications, users can increasingly describe what they want to achieve.

Imagine a typical business scenario:

Instead of opening multiple reports and manually compiling data, a user could ask:

“Analyze sales performance over the past three months, identify the largest deviations, and summarize the most important areas for action.”

The vision is for AI to help users find information, analyze data, and prepare decisions – and, depending on available capabilities and permissions, also assist in executing tasks.

People will spend less time searching for information and more time interpreting it and making the right decisions.

An important point: Not every task can already be fully automated. The actual benefits depend on the available capabilities, integration with business processes, and the quality of the underlying data.

4. The Real Change Is About People

The evolution of the SAP user interface is therefore not just a story about technology.

It is also a story about how our work is changing.

Era What matters most What it means for people

SAP GUITransactions and screensSystem knowledge and process expertise are essential
SAP FioriApps and tasksMore intuitive interaction and easier access to information
Joule Work and AIIntent, context, and assistanceGreater focus on analysis, decisions, and collaboration

This evolution raises important questions.

Which skills will become more important in the future?

Knowledge of individual transactions will remain valuable in many areas. At the same time, other skills will become increasingly important: asking the right questions, critically evaluating results, understanding business processes, and using AI effectively.

The roles of IT departments, SAP consultants, and process owners are also changing. It is no longer just about configuring systems correctly and training users. Increasingly, it is about designing intelligent workflows, making meaningful use of data, and helping people adapt to a new world of work.

And this is where a major challenge lies: New technology alone does not change the way people work. Real value is created only when people understand, trust, and use it effectively.

5. What Does This Mean for SAP Transformations?

For companies, one important insight emerges: The evolution of the user interface should not be treated as an isolated IT project.

Organizations modernizing SAP should also rethink their workflows, employee roles, data quality, and opportunities for automation.

Some key questions to consider:

  • Which tasks can be simplified through better user experience and guidance?

  • Where can AI assistants make information available more quickly?

  • Which processes are suitable for further automation?

  • How can we ensure that employees understand and embrace the new possibilities?

  • How do we measure whether productivity, quality, and employee satisfaction are actually improving?

Especially in the SAP ecosystem, it will be crucial to develop technology, processes, and people together.

Because a modern interface is not an end in itself. It must make work easier, better, and more meaningful.

Conclusion: Less Time Operating Systems. More Time Making an Impact.

From SAP GUI through SAP Fiori to Joule Work, we are witnessing an evolution that goes far beyond the design of a user interface.

We are moving from a world where people had to learn how to operate the system, through a world of intuitive, task-oriented applications, towards a way of working in which AI increasingly understands, assists, and supports tasks.

The exciting question is therefore no longer just what the next SAP interface will look like.

The real question is: How much more can people achieve when technology takes some of the complexity off their shoulders?

The future of SAP will not be measured solely by how intelligent the systems become. It will be measured by how effectively they help people make better decisions, collaborate more efficiently, and focus on what truly matters.

Less complexity. More intelligence. More time for what really matters.

#SAP #SAPFiori #Joule #JouleWork #SAPTransformation #AI #UserExperience #DigitalTransformation

entry.title: Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation
entry.content:
In a previous post we looked at connecting a custom A2A agent to S/4HANA Public Cloud with full principal propagation. But that approach comes with some drawbacks: hooking up individual APIs doesn't scale well, and it's hard to enforce governance. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for exposing tools and data to AI agents in a uniform way, and it's quickly becoming the common language between agents and enterprise systems. SAP's reference architecture for Agents and MCP positions Integration Suite as an MCP Gateway to safeguard traffic to enterprise systems — so this post extends the example to route a BTP-based agent through that gateway, still from customer-managed Joule.

Note: This post covers Customer-Managed Joule.

Scenario

We have an A2A-capable agent connected to Joule (customer-managed), with a destination that hands the Joule user's token to the agent on each A2A request. To reach S/4HANA Public Cloud, that agent now goes through the MCP Gateway: Integration Suite points its gateway at an S/4HANA OData service via a destination, the selected endpoints become MCP tools, and it all runs on Integration Cell. The user identity is propagated the whole way — from Joule, through the custom agent, through the MCP Gateway, into S/4HANA — so the backend call runs as the real user. And because the gateway sits on Integration Suite, we inherit the API Management controls we already know: additional authentication and authorization on top, plus IP filtering, rate limiting and quotas where we need them.

This matters because many customers have built their agents in an A2A manner, and their API policy often restricts them to endorsed architectures only.

Prerequisites

  • A working A2A agent and destination setup, as described in the principal propagation post
  • An S/4HANA Public Cloud system
  • Integration Suite, Enhanced Edition (only that Edition contains the MCP Gateway)

Step 1: Trust the Integration Suite subaccount in S/4

The very first step diverges from the previous post: the trust setup. Last time we configured S/4 to trust the destination certificate of the agent's subaccount. This time the piece that resolves the SAML Bearer assertion is the destination service of the subaccount where Integration Suite lives — and that is a different subaccount, with a different signing certificate (at least in my case). So we repeat the communication setup against that subaccount.

Concretely, in your Integration Suite subaccount go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust and grab the .pem. It is a self-signed cert whose subject looks like cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/<subaccount-id> with OU=CP Destination Configuration — this is the destination-service signing certificate.

Then, exactly as in the principal propagation post, set up a communication user, a communication system and a communication arrangement (SAP_COM_0008 for Business Partner) in S/4 — but upload this certificate under the communication system's OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider, and copy its subject CN into the Provider Name field.

Note: if the trust is missing or points at the wrong subaccount, the SAML exchange later fails with a very explicit "There is no trust between entities … in client 100". That message contains the subaccount ID it actually saw, which makes it easy to tell that you trusted the wrong one.

Step 2: Create the S/4HANA SAML Bearer destination in the IS subaccount

Next, create an HTTP destination toward S/4HANA in the subaccount where Integration Suite resides. This is the same OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion destination as in the previous post — the MCP server will use it as its target. The important properties:

Name=S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap
Audience=https://my3xxxxx.s4hana.cloud.sap
Token Service URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/bc/sec/oauth2/token
Client Key / Token Service User=<the comm user from step 1>
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:X509
userIdSource=mail
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

# additional properties
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs
IntegrationCell.Include=true

Two things that are easy to miss:

  • x_user_token.jwks_uri points at the IAS tenant so the destination service can validate the forwarded end-user token and build the SAML assertion for the real user. Without it, it silently falls back to a technical-user assertion and propagation breaks.
  • IntegrationCell.Include=true is a label on the destination. Without it the destination simply won't appear in the MCP Server wizard's dropdown at all.

Step 3: Build the MCP server in Integration Suite

Now the new part. In Design → Integrations and APIs, create an integration package to hold the artifact.

Inside the package, add an MCP Server artifact. The wizard's first step asks for the source type — pick HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification:

In the next step, point it at the S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST destination with a relative URL of /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER, give it a name and an MCP Path (e.g. /s4_bp_mcp), and leave the runtime profile on Integration Cell:

Skip the AI spec generation. Once the artifact exists, open its MCP Configuration → Source tab and hit Edit API Specification to supply the spec:

Import the OpenAPI/EDMX of the Business Partner service — you can download it from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, or just pull the live $metadata from your own system:

On the Tools tab, select the operations you want to expose; each one becomes an MCP tool. I started with a single GET A_BusinessPartner → the tool get_A_BusinessPartner. Keep it small; the model routes better with fewer, well-described tools:

The tricky part is the inbound security — this is where the whole principal-propagation story lives. On the Policies tab every MCP server has a mandatory Authentication and Authorization policy, so we look at both.

Authentication

The Authentication policy decides which tokens the gateway trusts. By default an MCP server validates tokens issued through the Integration Suite subaccount's own XSUAA / the IdP configured there. That default path is enough for a client like Joule Work Desktop, which runs its own user-token fetch flow against that trusted authorization server when you add the connector — so the end-user identity is already there, you don't configure anything extra on the gateway.

Our case is different: the token doesn't come from a JWD connector, it's the JWT our A2A agent forwards from Joule, issued by our IAS tenant — and a raw token from that issuer is rejected by the default policy with 401 invalidToken because the gateway doesn't trust it yet.

The fix is to switch the Authentication policy to External OAuth (OIDC) and point it at our IAS tenant. Even though this feels a bit strange — our IAS tenant is treated as an "external" OAuth provider here — the "internal" option is the subaccount's XSUAA, which may well itself be configured to redirect logins to exactly that same IAS. So "external" just means: validate the token directly against the IAS tenant, by its own issuer and keys.

Once External OAuth is selected, there are four fields to fill:

Field Value

Well-Known URLhttps://<ias-tenant>/.well-known/openid-configuration
Audiencethe aud of the token the client actually sends (see the gotcha below)
ClientID Key${authn.oidc.jwt.azp}
UserInfo Key${authn.oidc.jwt.mail}

What these actually do: the Well-Known URL tells the gateway which IAS tenant to trust — it discovers the issuer and the signing keys from there, and validates every incoming token's signature against them. The Audience is the gateway saying "I only accept tokens that were actually meant for this application" — it's matched against the token's aud claim. ClientID Key and UserInfo Key are expressions that tell the gateway which claims carry the calling client's ID (azp) and the end user's identity (mail) — the latter being exactly the identity that gets propagated downstream.

The Audience is the one that'll bite you. Our destination maps userIdSource=mail, and the token that eventually arrives is the one Joule forwarded — i.e. after its app-to-app exchange — so its aud is the Custom Agent App client ID, not the login app you used to get a test token. You find that client ID in your IAS admin console under Applications → your Custom Agent App → Client ID (it's the same value that your agent already validates as its IAS_AUDIENCE). If you set the policy audience to the wrong app, the real Joule token is rejected with 401 invalidToken even though everything else is correct. You can also list multiple audiences comma-separated, or leave it empty to skip audience validation entirely while debugging.

If authentication is not configured correctly, the gateway rejects the call before it ever reaches your backend — a decoded IAS token that doesn't match issuer/audience comes back as:

{ "error": { "code": "invalidToken", "message": "Unable to authenticate user, invalid token" } }

(HTTP 401)

Authorization

The second mandatory policy is Authorization — and this is where it helps to understand how an IAS token is built, because it is fundamentally different from the XSUAA token you may be used to.

An XSUAA access token carries a scope claim (things like myapp.Read, API.invoke), and the default Authorization policy checks exactly that: does the token contain the required scope? An IAS token has no scope claim at all. IAS is an identity provider — it answers "who are you", not "what may you do"; the actual authorization is expected to happen in the target system (the user's S/4 roles, in our case). A decoded IAS user token has mail, sub, azp — but nothing a scope-based policy can match on.

What an IAS token does carry, because it came through Joule's app-to-app exchange, is the ias_apis claim — a list of the exposed APIs the user is allowed to call:

{
  "iss": "https://<ias-tenant>",
  "aud": "<custom-agent-app client id>",
  "azp": "<proxy-app client id>",
  "mail": "felix.bartler@sap.com",
  "ias_apis": ["a2a_custom_agent_app_api"]
}

So the configuration change versus the XSUAA default is: don't check a scope claim, check the ias_apis list instead. Point the Authorization policy's Scope Key at ias_apis and set the expected value to our exposed API:

Authorization field Value

Authorization TypeOAuth Scope OR Developer Key
Scope Keyias_apis
Scopea2a_custom_agent_app_api

The policy then checks whether the ias_apis list contains a2a_custom_agent_app_api — which doubles as a useful access gate: it enforces, right at the gateway, that only users entitled to this agent's exposed API can call it at all.

If authorization is wrong — e.g. the policy still checks scope, which an IAS token doesn't have — the gateway authenticates the user fine but then refuses the operation:

{ "error": { "code": "forbidden", "message": "User doesn't have the authorization to perform this operation" } }

(HTTP 403)

With both policies right, the gateway accepts the real Joule user token, validates it against IAS, reads mail, and forwards the identity to the destination.

Deploy MCP Server

Finally Deploy onto the Integration Cell runtime, and once the Runtime Status reads STARTED the MCP URL is live:

We've basically turned an OData endpoint into a proper MCP Server — with a curated list of tools — and put an auth layer in front of it that enforces principal propagation. Let's test it:

Testing the gateway with curl

Before touching any agent code, it's worth proving the gateway end to end in isolation — exactly like the SAML dry-run in the previous post. MCP over Streamable HTTP is just JSON-RPC over HTTP, so three curl calls do it: initialize (which returns an mcp-session-id response header you must echo back), notifications/initialized, then tools/call.

# USER_JWT = a REAL Joule-forwarded token (see the caveat below), MCP_URL = the deployed MCP server URL

# 1) initialize — grab the mcp-session-id straight from the response header
SID=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%header{mcp-session-id}' -X POST "$MCP_URL" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"}}}')

# 2) say "initialized"
curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}'

# 3) call the tool as the user (note: OData options without `$`, select is an ARRAY)
curl -s -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_A_BusinessPartner","arguments":{"top":3,"select":["BusinessPartner","BusinessPartnerName"]}}}'

This is the fastest feedback loop for getting the two policies right — the error you get back tells you exactly which stage failed: 401 invalidToken = authentication (issuer/audience), 403 forbidden = authorization (scope/ias_apis), real OData rows = success.

Getting a token that actually works for the test. A plain IAS password grant gives you a token audienced for the login app and without ias_apis, so it fails both audience and authorization — it is not a stand-in for what Joule sends. You have two options to get a realistic token:

  1. Reproduce the app-to-app exchange yourself. This is exactly what Joule does internally: take the user token and exchange it (via the jwt-bearer grant against your IAS, using the proxy app's client credentials and the proxy-to-target dependency) into a token audienced for the Custom Agent App — which then carries ias_apis. If you own the proxy app's credentials, this is the clean, scriptable way and the one I'd recommend for a proper test harness.
  2. Capture a real one. Quicker for a one-off: temporarily log the raw Authorization header in your agent, prompt Joule once, and copy the forwarded JWT out of the logs.

Step 4: The Python agent that calls the MCP gateway

The change on the agent side is small and local: the one place that used to call the destination service and S/4 directly (s4_client.py in the previous post) is replaced by a small MCP client. Everything else — the LangGraph tool, the executor, the IAS middleware on the agent's own inbound endpoint — stays as it was.

The MCP client uses Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC to call the MCP Gateway. This is part of the standard of MCP - and one could also use a SDK. We do 3 calls: initialize (which hands back an mcp-session-id response header you carry on every following request), notifications/initialized, and tools/call:

# mcp_client.py (abridged)
def call_business_partner_api(user_jwt, top=10, select=None, filter_expr=None, ...):
    session_id = _open_session(user_jwt)        # initialize -> mcp-session-id
    r = requests.post(
        MCP_URL,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {user_jwt}",   # <-- the whole trick
            "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream",
            "mcp-session-id": session_id,
        },
        json={
            "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
            "params": {
                "name": "get_A_BusinessPartner",
                "arguments": {"top": top, "select": [...]},   # OData options, no `$`, select is an array
            },
        },
    )
    # tool output comes back as result.content[0].text (JSON string of the OData payload)

The user_jwt it forwards is the exact same token the agent already extracts from the inbound A2A request — unchanged from the previous post:

# agent_executor.py — the token comes straight from the Authorization header Joule sent
auth = context._call_context.state.get("headers", {}).get("authorization", "")
user_jwt = auth[len("bearer "):] if auth.lower().startswith("bearer ") else None
# ... threaded down to the tool, which puts it on the MCP call as Authorization: Bearer

The key point: the agent needs no credentials of its own for the backend. No client secret, no destination binding to S/4 — just the MCP_URL of the deployed gateway. It takes the user's token and passes it on; IAS, the gateway and the destination service do the rest. (The agent's own inbound A2A endpoint is still protected by the IAS middleware exactly as before.)

Two details are worth knowing when calling an Integration-Suite-generated tool: the handshake is session-based (echo the mcp-session-id header after initialize), and the generated tool schema uses OData options without the leading $, with select/expand/orderby as arrays of strings — pass a comma-separated string and the call fails schema validation.

Test in Joule

Deploy the agent, point Joule's agent destination at it, and prompt it — e.g. "show me business partners that start with I". The full chain runs: the agent forwards the user's token to the gateway, the gateway validates it against IAS, propagates the signed-in user through the SAML Bearer destination, and S/4HANA returns exactly the records that user is authorized to see, rendered as a table in the conversation:

This is the point of the whole exercise: the data comes back scoped to the real signed-in user, propagated all the way from Joule to S/4HANA — exactly the behaviour we wanted. And because it now runs through the gateway, we can also see it happen: in Integration Suite under Monitor → Integrations and APIs → Monitor Message Processing (with the Integration Cell runtime selected), each prompt shows up as a BusinessPartnerMCP entry of type MCP Server, status Completed. That's the proof the call actually traversed the MCP gateway rather than some direct backchannel — and the governance, tracing and policy enforcement that come with it apply to every call.

Conclusion

Looks good. We have the full flow in place and can use the MCP Gateway for our A2A Agents. Hope you found this insightful.

The full code is on GitHub under a2a_pp_mcp_gateway/.

This post is part of the Joule A2A series:

  • Connect code-based agents into Joule
  • Secure code-based agents with IAS
  • Handling multi-turn conversations
  • Building custom Joule capabilities: message types in practice
  • Propagate the user identity from Joule into S/4HANA
  • MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation (this post)

The essential takeaway: SAP-managed is not a new product customers purchase. It's a shift in the provisioning model. The result is a clear division of responsibility – partners lead with business innovation, while SAP manages the Joule configuration and runtime platform. This is different from the customer-managed SAP BTP provisioning that partners navigated through the SAP BTP Cockpit.


Why this matters for partners

SAP is taking ownership of the time-consuming provisioning and configuration tasks – giving customers faster time to value and partners more time to focus on delivering high-value business outcomes.

Partners typically include a setup fee in their service engagements. With SAP-managed provisioning for Joule, that setup effort shrinks dramatically – but that time doesn’t disappear, it gets redirected. With setup and configuration time dropping considerably, it frees up resources to move toward innovation, value-added services, and deeper customer engagement. This means:

  • Faster project starts and shorter deployment cycles
  • Less time on platform administration, more time delivering measurable customer value
  • More focus on differentiated IP, industry accelerators, and custom agents
  • Higher-margin engagements centered on process transformation, change management, and business outcomes


Every customer has a clear path forward

Regardless of where a customer is on their journey, there is a defined path to SAP-managed provisioning for Joule:

  • Net-new customers: Activate directly through SAP for Me from day one under the SAP-managed model
  • Existing Joule Studio Classic customers: Migration resources will become available in 2027


Get ready now

Shift your practice from activation and infrastructure to agent development and customer value delivery. Partners can have confident conversations at any stage of the customer journey.

entry.title: How to Enable SAP Joule for SAP SuccessFactors Using SAP BTP and Cloud Identity Services
entry.content:
1. Understanding the Architecture

For a SuccessFactors implementation, the Joule landscape can be viewed in three layers.

Experience Layer

The user works primarily in SAP SuccessFactors.

Joule is embedded into the SuccessFactors user experience. Users don't need to leave SuccessFactors simply to interact with Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

Conceptually:

Employee / Manager → SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule

AI and Platform Layer

Although Joule appears inside SuccessFactors, Joule itself runs as a service on SAP BTP. [https://le...essfactors]

SAP SuccessFactors continues to own the HR business data and processes, while Joule provides the conversational and orchestration layer.

Conceptually:

SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule → SAP BTP

Identity and Authorization Layer

The third area is identity and authorization.

SAP Cloud Identity Services forms part of the Joule identity architecture, while SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions determine which SuccessFactors information and functionality a user is authorized to access. [https://le...essfactors]

This separation is important. Enabling Joule does not give the user unrestricted access to SuccessFactors.

2. Check the Prerequisites

Before configuring anything, start by validating that your landscape satisfies SAP's Joule prerequisites.

SAP's Setting Up Joule for SAP SuccessFactors Learning content lists prerequisites including:

  • SAP BTP account with the required Joule entitlement
  • Joule entitlement identified as das-application
  • SAP SuccessFactors license
  • Joule availability for the applicable data center
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants
  • SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start [https://le...essfactors]

The last prerequisite is worth noting.

Your users may access Joule directly from the SuccessFactors experience and may not use a separate SAP Build Work Zone site as their business launchpad. Nevertheless, SAP's current Learning material lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start among the prerequisites for the overall Joule setup. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, don't interpret "using SuccessFactors as the launchpad" as meaning that all SAP Start / Build Work Zone platform dependencies can simply be omitted.

Follow the dependencies presented by the Joule onboarding process for your particular landscape.

3. Check the Required Administrator Access

Before starting the implementation, make sure the configuration team has the required administrative access.

SAP's SuccessFactors Joule setup guidance identifies the following administrative roles:

  • SAP SuccessFactors Administrator
  • SAP BTP Global Account Administrator
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services Administrator [https://he...cale=en-US]

This is important because the onboarding isn't limited to SuccessFactors configuration. It crosses the SuccessFactors, BTP and identity landscapes.

At this stage, your initial checklist should therefore be:

  • SuccessFactors tenant and license are available
  • SAP BTP Global Account is identified
  • Joule entitlement is available
  • Appropriate SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants are available
  • Required administrators have access
  • Joule availability for the relevant landscape/data center has been checked
  • SAP Start / Build Work Zone requirement has been assessed according to the current Joule onboarding model

4. Verify the Joule Entitlement in SAP BTP

The next step is to verify that the SAP BTP Global Account has the required Joule entitlement.

SAP Learning specifically identifies the Joule entitlement as:

das-application

SAP recommends checking the entitlements available in the BTP Global Account. [https://le...essfactors]

If you have the appropriate SuccessFactors license but the Joule entitlement isn't available, SAP Learning advises contacting your SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Don't try to compensate for a missing Joule entitlement by manually creating unrelated BTP services. Resolve the commercial/provisioning issue first.

A successful implementation starts with the correct entitlement being delivered to the correct SAP BTP Global Account.

5. Prepare SAP Cloud Identity Services

Once the commercial and BTP prerequisites are established, the next major area is identity.

SAP Learning explicitly lists SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants as a prerequisite for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

Before starting Joule onboarding, document the participating systems and identity landscape.

At minimum, identify:

  • SAP SuccessFactors tenant
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant
  • SAP BTP Global Account
  • Relevant BTP landscape
  • Production versus non-production systems
  • User identities used across the participating systems

This might seem administrative, but it becomes extremely useful when troubleshooting authentication and user provisioning.

A common source of confusion is treating IAS and IPS as though they perform the same function. They should be considered separately.

6. Understand IAS: Identity Authentication

SAP Identity Authentication is part of SAP Cloud Identity Services.

From an implementation perspective, think about Identity Authentication as the authentication side of the architecture.

The central question is:

How is the identity of the user established across the participating SAP applications?

Your Joule implementation therefore needs to consider how SuccessFactors, Joule/BTP and SAP Cloud Identity Services participate in establishing a consistent user identity.

SAP's Learning material identifies active SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants as part of the prerequisites for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

The exact configuration should follow the Joule onboarding guidance appropriate to your tenant rather than assuming a generic IAS configuration will be sufficient.

7. Understand IPS: Identity Provisioning

Authentication isn't the whole identity story.

The second area is Identity Provisioning Service (IPS).

Conceptually:

IAS answers the authentication/identity question.

IPS deals with provisioning identities between the relevant systems.

SAP's Joule provisioning documentation explicitly includes Configure Identity Provisioning Service within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Therefore, don't document your implementation simply as "IAS configured."

Your architecture documentation should separately record:

Authentication

How users authenticate and how their identities are established across the participating applications.

Provisioning

How identities required by the Joule landscape are provisioned and synchronized.

The actual source, target and provisioning configuration should follow the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the landscape being implemented.

8. Start the Official Joule Onboarding Process

Once the prerequisites, BTP entitlement and Cloud Identity Services landscape are ready, proceed with Joule onboarding.

This is an area where it is especially important not to follow an outdated blog containing a static list of destinations, service instances or role collections.

SAP's current SuccessFactors documentation directs administrators to:

Follow the Joule Onboarding Guide to finish the setup. [https://he...cale=en-US]

SAP Learning also points to SAP's activation guidance for implementing Joule with SuccessFactors. [https://le...essfactors]

Use the official onboarding process applicable to your system.

During this phase, validate that you are working with:

  • The intended BTP Global Account
  • The intended SuccessFactors system
  • The correct SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape
  • The required Joule entitlement
  • The appropriate production or non-production environment

Avoid manually reproducing configuration from an old implementation unless that configuration is still explicitly required by the current onboarding process.

9. Understand the Role of SAP Build Work Zone / SAP Start

This particular topic can create confusion for SuccessFactors customers.

In this implementation scenario, the end user experiences Joule through SAP SuccessFactors.

That does not mean you should automatically remove SAP Build Work Zone/SAP Start from the technical architecture.

SAP's current Learning material for setting up Joule with SuccessFactors explicitly lists:

SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start

among the prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

The accurate way to describe the architecture is therefore:

SuccessFactors is the user-facing business application from which users interact with Joule. The technical services and platform dependencies required by SAP's current Joule onboarding model are provisioned separately according to SAP's onboarding guidance.

This is particularly important if you're coming from an S/4HANA Cloud background.

Don't equate the user's launchpad with every underlying platform component used to deliver Joule.

10. Complete the SuccessFactors-Side Joule Setup

After completing the required Joule onboarding activities, move to the SuccessFactors-side configuration.

The critical concept here is that provisioning Joule doesn't automatically give every SuccessFactors user access to it.

You still need to control which users have permission to use Joule.

SAP's SuccessFactors documentation explicitly identifies an Access to Joule permission. [https://he...cale=en-US]

In SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions, the documented permission is located under:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Assign this permission through the appropriate SuccessFactors RBP roles according to the users who should have access to Joule.

This gives you a clear separation:

Technical onboarding enables the Joule service.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions control which SuccessFactors users can access Joule.

11. Existing SuccessFactors Authorizations Still Apply

Granting Access to Joule should not be confused with granting unrestricted access to SuccessFactors functionality.

SAP states that the business data and actions accessed through Joule continue to be governed by existing SuccessFactors authorizations. [https://le...essfactors]

This means two conditions need to be considered.

Condition 1: Joule access

Is the user authorized to access Joule?

Condition 2: Business authorization

Is the same user authorized in SuccessFactors to access the requested HR information or execute the requested business operation?

Both are important.

For example, enabling Joule for an employee should not be considered a mechanism for bypassing Role-Based Permissions protecting manager or HR information.

This is one of the most important design principles to explain to your security and HR authorization teams.

12. Configure Employee Central Quick Actions Where Applicable

If you're using SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central, there is another configuration area to review.

SAP recommends enabling Employee Central Quick Actions and configuring the corresponding templates for Employee Central customers using Joule. [https://he...cale=en-US]

The reason this is relevant is that Joule isn't purely a question-and-answer interface.

SAP's architecture description discusses Joule supporting conversational interaction involving navigation and transactional interactions in the business application. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, for Employee Central implementations, review the Quick Actions needed for the supported Joule use cases you intend to make available.

Don't assume that every Employee Central action automatically becomes available through Joule.

Always validate the particular use case against the current SuccessFactors Joule documentation.

13. Validate Joule in SAP SuccessFactors

Once the onboarding, identity configuration and SuccessFactors authorization settings are complete, validate the solution from the SuccessFactors experience.

Use a test user that has:

  • Access to Joule
  • Correct identity configuration
  • Appropriate SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Access to the underlying SuccessFactors functionality being tested

The first validation is simple:

Can the user access Joule from the SuccessFactors user experience?

If yes, don't stop there.

The next validation is:

Can Joule access only the SuccessFactors information and operations that this user is authorized to use?

SAP states that existing SuccessFactors authorizations govern the data and actions available through Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

That means functional and security validation should be performed together.

14. Test Different Authorization Scenarios

A good implementation should test more than one type of user.

Employee User

Use an employee account with normal Employee Self-Service permissions.

Validate the supported Joule scenarios applicable to employees.

Manager User

Use a manager account with appropriate manager permissions.

Validate supported manager scenarios where applicable.

Restricted User

Use an account intentionally lacking access to selected SuccessFactors information or functionality.

Validate that giving the user access to Joule doesn't extend the user's access beyond the underlying SuccessFactors authorization.

The purpose is not merely to prove that Joule opens successfully.

The purpose is to prove:

Joule availability + correct identity + correct SuccessFactors authorization + supported use case

work together.

15. Understand Which SuccessFactors Use Cases Are Supported

Another important implementation step is determining what you actually want users to do with Joule.

Not every SuccessFactors capability should be assumed to have a corresponding Joule capability.

SAP maintains documentation for the supported Joule capabilities and use cases within SuccessFactors. [https://he...essfactors]

For example, SAP's SuccessFactors Onboarding documentation lists scenarios such as:

  • Completing required onboarding tasks
  • Assigning a buddy
  • Viewing pending offboarding tasks
  • Directing new hires to their Onboarding Checklist and Onboarding Guide [https://he...cale=en-US]

This demonstrates why the business configuration underneath Joule remains important.

Having the Joule window available doesn't automatically make every HR operation available conversationally.

For any implementation, create a list of the specific SuccessFactors Joule use cases that your organization plans to enable and validate each against current SAP documentation.

16. End-to-End Implementation Sequence

Putting everything together, the recommended implementation flow is:

Step 1: Verify SuccessFactors prerequisites

Confirm the SuccessFactors licensing and applicable Joule prerequisites.

Step 2: Verify Joule availability

Check whether Joule is available for the applicable SuccessFactors landscape/data center according to the current SAP guidance. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 3: Verify the BTP Global Account

Confirm that you're working with the intended SAP BTP Global Account.

Step 4: Verify Joule entitlement

Check that the Joule das-application entitlement is available in the BTP landscape. [https://le...essfactors]

If the entitlement is missing for an appropriately licensed scenario, follow SAP's guidance and contact the SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 5: Establish the SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape

Identify the SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant participating in the implementation. SAP lists active Cloud Identity Services tenants among the SuccessFactors Joule prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 6: Address authentication

Follow the Joule onboarding guidance for the required Identity Authentication configuration.

Step 7: Address identity provisioning

Configure the required Identity Provisioning integration according to the current onboarding flow. SAP's Joule provisioning documentation includes Identity Provisioning configuration within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 8: Complete Joule onboarding

Follow the official Joule Onboarding Guide, as directed by SAP's SuccessFactors documentation. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 9: Handle SAP Start / Build Work Zone dependencies

Implement the applicable platform dependency according to the Joule onboarding model. SAP's current Learning content lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start as a prerequisite. [https://le...essfactors]

This doesn't mean users must use a separate Work Zone site as their SuccessFactors launchpad.

Step 10: Configure SuccessFactors Joule access

Grant the relevant SuccessFactors users:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 11: Review SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions

Ensure users have the underlying SuccessFactors authorization required by each business use case. Joule continues to operate within these authorization boundaries. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 12: Configure Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

For Employee Central scenarios, review and configure the Quick Actions recommended by SAP. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 13: Validate Joule

Test Joule from the SAP SuccessFactors user experience.

Step 14: Validate business use cases

Test the actual supported employee and manager use cases required by your organization.

Step 15: Validate authorization boundaries

Confirm that Joule respects the underlying SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

17. Troubleshooting Approach

If Joule isn't working after configuration, troubleshoot the solution layer by layer instead of changing multiple components simultaneously.

Joule isn't available at all

First verify:

  • Joule entitlement
  • BTP landscape
  • Joule onboarding completion
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

User can't access Joule

Verify:

  • User identity
  • Relevant Cloud Identity Services configuration
  • Identity provisioning
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

Joule opens but a business request doesn't work

Verify:

  • Whether that particular Joule use case is supported
  • User's SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Required SuccessFactors business configuration
  • Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

This layer-by-layer troubleshooting method is my recommended implementation approach. The individual requirements above should still be validated against the current SAP onboarding documentation.

18. Final Implementation Checklist

Before declaring the solution ready, validate the following.

Licensing and Landscape

  • SuccessFactors license verified
  • Joule availability verified
  • Correct BTP Global Account identified
  • Correct landscape selected
  • Joule das-application entitlement available

Identity

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services available
  • Authentication requirements completed according to Joule onboarding
  • Identity provisioning requirements completed
  • User identity is consistent across the participating landscape

Joule

  • Official Joule onboarding completed
  • Required platform services provisioned
  • SuccessFactors integration completed

SuccessFactors

  • Access to Joule permission assigned
  • Target users correctly included in RBP roles
  • Underlying SuccessFactors permissions validated
  • Employee Central Quick Actions configured where applicable

Validation

  • Joule accessible from SuccessFactors
  • Employee scenario validated
  • Manager scenario validated where applicable
  • Restricted-user scenario validated
  • RBP authorization boundaries confirmed
  • Required SuccessFactors Joule use cases tested

Conclusion

The most important point when implementing Joule for SAP SuccessFactors is understanding that this isn't simply a switch inside SuccessFactors.

The implementation spans multiple layers:

SAP SuccessFactors provides the HR business application and remains the system of record.

SAP Joule on SAP BTP provides the conversational AI and orchestration experience.

SAP Cloud Identity Services participates in the identity architecture.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions continue to control access to HR data and business functionality. [https://le...essfactors]

For users, however, the experience can remain straightforward: they interact with Joule from SAP SuccessFactors while the underlying BTP and identity landscape provides the services required to enable that experience.

For implementation teams, the safest sequence is therefore:

Prerequisites → Entitlement → Identity → Provisioning → Joule Onboarding → SuccessFactors Permissions → Quick Actions → Business Use Cases → Security Validation

Most importantly, always use the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the tenant being implemented instead of relying exclusively on older manual configuration procedures. SAP's current SuccessFactors documentation explicitly directs administrators to the Joule Onboarding Guide for setup. [https://he...cale=en-US]

entry.title: What If Joule Could Help You Complete the Business-Driven Configuration Questionnaire? Now It Can.
entry.content:
A successful SAP S/4HANA Cloud implementation starts with understanding how a business works—and translating that understanding into the right configuration. The Business-Driven Configuration Questionnaire (BDCQ), a structured accelerator within the SAP Activate methodology, helps make that connection. Line of Business (LoB) configuration experts use it to gather the configuration values that will ultimately be entered in SAP Central Business Configuration for the customer’s SAP S/4HANA Cloud development system tenants.

More than a questionnaire, the BDCQ is a bridge between SAP consultants and customer business users. It helps ensure that solution configuration reflects real business requirements, both before and during Fit-to-Standard workshops.

Why does the BDCQ matter?

  • It provides early insight into the customer’s business processes and configuration needs.
  • It offers prescriptive guidance on identifying configuration requirements aligned with the implementation scope.
  • It provides a secondary validation of whether SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (Public Cloud) is the right fit for the customer, complementing the Digital Discovery Assessment (DDA).
  • It brings greater structure to the planning and delivery of Fit-to-Standard Analysis workshops.
  • It supports productive conversations between implementation experts and business users during workshops.
  • It connects customer business processes directly to solution configuration activities, including references to specific SSCUI apps or SSCUI groups.

The BDCQ captures two levels of information at different stages of the project:

The value of the BDCQ goes beyond collecting configuration data. It also helps LoB configuration experts build relationships with customer LoB experts and introduces those experts to SAP S/4HANA Cloud early in the project. Ideally, the same customer experts who provide L2 responses will take part in Fit-to-Standard workshops and user acceptance testing before go-live. In this way, the BDCQ also supports the project’s broader change-management effort.

Not every BDCQ maps neatly to a traditional line of business. The implementation team should therefore confirm that all business processes selected in the Digital Discovery Assessment are covered across the available BDCQs. Any remaining processes—for example, Human Resources or Two-Tier ERP—should be assigned based on transferable expertise and team availability.

So, how can AI-assisted support make it easier to complete the BDCQ?

During the Prepare phase, open Perform Initial Business Process Assessment for SAP S/4HANA Cloud. You’ll find the ✦ AI-Assisted Procedure session there.

Open the session and follow the instructions for working with the BDCQ Experts.

For example, the BDCQ-FI Expert can guide you through the questionnaire in a conversational manner. Start the conversation, answer its questions, and review the highlights and key points that deserve attention. This provides structured support as you work through the information required for your BDCQ.

The result is a BDCQ populated with Critical Steps, Scope Items, open items, and potential blockers—as illustrated in the example below.

entry.title: Did You Know? An SAP Business Data Cloud Series | Season 1, Episode 3 | Joule for Datasphere
entry.content:
Your AI Copilot Is Already Inside SAP Datasphere... Are You Using It? 

Here's something a lot of SAP Datasphere users don't realize: Joule, SAP's generative AI copilot, is embedded directly in Datasphere. Not in a separate tool, but directly in the platform you're already working on every day. 

Many data professionals associate Joule with SAP S/4HANA or SAP Analytics Cloud. And while Joule is also present in those products, its integration with Datasphere is one of the more quietly powerful capabilities in your SAP Business Data Cloud environment. 

What is Joule for Datasphere? 

Joule in Datasphere supports three categories of tasks: informational, navigational, and transactional. Together, they cover a meaningful slice of the day-to-day work data professionals do inside the tool. 

Informational: Ask Joule how to use a specific Datasphere feature and get an answer grounded in product documentation without leaving the platform to hunt through help pages or community posts. You can also query Joule for instance-specific information about your own Datasphere environment. 

Navigational: Joule can guide you through tasks and help you move around the platform more efficiently. For newer team members or occasional users, this can significantly reduce the learning curve. 

Transactional: This is where it gets genuinely interesting for data engineers and modelers. Joule supports AI-assisted SQL generation directly in the SQL View Builder. This means that you can describe what you want in natural language, and Joule generates the SQL. Whether you're creating a new SQL view from scratch or modifying an existing one, this capability can meaningfully cut down the time spent writing and debugging queries. 

Joule also supports AI-assisted semantic generation, automatically recognizing and assigning semantic types for ingested non-SAP data, which is typically a manual and time-consuming preparation step. 

Why it Matters to Data Professionals 

The honest reality of working with data at scale is that a significant portion of the time goes into maintenance tasks: figuring out the right syntax, navigating documentation, writing boilerplate SQL, manually classifying fields. These tasks take valuable time out of your day and eat into time that could be spent making strategic business decisions. Joule helps give you that time back! It doesn't replace your judgment, but rather it takes on the mechanical parts, so you can focus on the work that actually requires your expertise. 

For data modelers, the SQL generation capability alone is worth exploring. For enterprise architects managing complex environments with many users at different skill levels, the informational and navigational capabilities help teams work more independently and consistently. 

Why You May Have Missed It 

Joule in Datasphere needs to be activated at the tenant level and requires users to have the appropriate privilege assigned. It doesn't switch on automatically. That setup step means a lot of teams have Joule available but haven't enabled it, or have enabled it without communicating it to the people who would benefit most. 

If you're a Datasphere administrator reading this, it's worth checking whether Joule is active in your environment and whether your modelers and data engineers know it's there. 

See It in Action

Give it a try in your own environment and see how much of your workflow it can simplify.

entry.title: SAP CPQ : The Future of Sales Quoting Is Here: Meet SAP's Joule Quoting Assistant & Other Agents
entry.content:
Disclaimer: : The purpose of this blog is to share a custom implementation approach for automating sales processes in SAP CPQ using Joule Work and Joule Studio. This content is aimed at customers and partners interested in innovation and automation scenarios.  
If you would like to explore these capabilities, please enroll in the EAC program and connect with your SAP CSM, CSP, or Account Executive to discuss available options.

Also please watch out for the Official SAP CPQ Product Roadmap items for Joule Assistants Delivery and What's New for SAP CPQ releases time to time.

How AI is transforming one of sales' most time-consuming processes

Every sales rep knows the pain. A customer sends over an email — or a ten-page PDF — and suddenly you're spending the better part of your afternoon manually parsing the request, matching products, checking pricing rules, and assembling a proposal document. It's repetitive, error-prone, and it gets in the way of actual selling.

SAP's Joule Quoting Assistant & remaining 6 other Agents is designed to change that entirely.

What Is the Joule Quoting Assistant?

The Joule Quoting Assistant is an AI-powered Joule Assistant — part of SAP's broader agentic AI portfolio — built specifically for the quote-to-order cycle. Its core mission: transform unstructured customer requests into accurate, compliant quotes with AI-guided selling across the entire SAP CPQ (Configure, Price, Quote) flow. Source

It sits at the intersection of SAP CPQ, SAP Sales Cloud, and SAP S/4HANA, orchestrating specialized AI agents behind the scenes to handle tasks that would otherwise fall to the sales rep or a back-office support team.

From Inbox to Quote: What It Actually Does

Here's where the Quoting Assistant gets practical. Given an unstructured customer inquiry — whether it arrives as an email, a request for quotation (RFQ), or a PDF — the assistant can:

  • Convert the raw request into a structured CPQ quote draft, extracting relevant intent and mapping it to your product catalog and pricing rules.
  • Recommend compliant product configurations based on what the customer described in natural language — no need to manually navigate complex configurators.
  • Surface real-time upsell, add-on, and cross-sell options guided by historical deal data and pricing policies.
  • Assemble proposal documents and draft customer-facing emails, ready for the rep to review and send.
  • Route multi-step requests to the right specialized agents automatically, without manual handoffs.
  • Enforce pricing and discount policies — every quote stays within guardrails, reducing approvals overhead and compliance risk. Source

Why This Matters for your Sales Teams

The shift from manual quoting to AI-guided quoting isn't just about speed — it changes the quality and consistency of the entire sales conversation.

Faster time to first draft. Instead of spending hours building a quote from scratch, reps get an intelligent draft that's already shaped by the customer's actual request. That frees them up to focus on relationship management and deal strategy.

Better accuracy and compliance. When pricing rules, discount limits, and configuration constraints are embedded in the assistant's reasoning, errors are caught before they reach the customer — not after an internal audit.

Higher deal size through guided selling. Real-time upsell and cross-sell recommendations aren't an afterthought; they're built into the quoting flow. Reps are prompted with relevant options at exactly the right moment.

Tighter SAP ecosystem integration. The Quoting Assistant works natively within SAP CPQ and SAP S/4HANA, which means no data re-entry, clean-core alignment, and full traceability across the quote lifecycle. Source

The Architecture Behind It: Assistants + Agents

The Quoting Assistant doesn't work alone. It's part of SAP's layered AI architecture: Joule Assistants — role-aligned, context-aware AI systems — sit above Joule Agents, which are the task specialists that execute individual steps. Source

You tell the Quoting Assistant what you want to accomplish in plain language. It interprets your intent, pulls in your business context (your CPQ rules, your pricing policies, your customer history), and coordinates the agents doing the actual work. You stay in control; the heavy lifting happens automatically.

This architecture is important because it means the Quoting Assistant isn't a standalone tool — it's part of SAP's Autonomous Enterprise vision, where AI handles routine execution so people can focus on decisions that require judgment.

A Real-World Scenario

Imagine a key account manager receives an email from a customer requesting a customised bundle of hardware and professional services across three countries, with specific delivery windows and a tight margin requirement.

Historically, this would take hours — coordinating with product management, pricing, and legal before a quote could even be drafted.

With the Joule Quoting Assistant, the rep pastes (or forwards) the customer email, and the assistant:

  1. Parses the request and maps it to available products and service SKUs.
  2. Checks configuration rules and flags any incompatible options.
  3. Proposes a compliant price structure with margin guardrails.
  4. Recommends a maintenance bundle and a support tier upsell.
  5. Drafts the proposal document and a personalised cover email.

The rep reviews, adjusts, approves. What took half a day now takes minutes.

What This Signals for the Future of Sales

SAP's investment in the Quoting Assistant reflects a broader industry shift: the sales rep of the near future is a reviewer and relationship manager, not a data entry clerk. AI handles the structure; humans handle the nuance.

For organisations running SAP CPQ or SAP Sales Cloud v2, this isn't a distant roadmap item — it's available now, and it integrates with the systems you already have. The question isn't whether to evaluate it; it's how quickly you can get it into the hands of your team.

The SAP Joule Quoting Assistant is part of the SAP Joule Assistants portfolio. Learn more at sap.com/use-cases/joule-assistant/quoting-ai.
