entry.title: From static plans to a “planning brain”: how SAP planning agents can reshape Enterprise Planning
entry.content:
Introduction

The opportunity with planning agents is not simply to produce forecasts faster. It is to connect the work of preparing data, building models, investigating performance, evaluating scenarios and communicating decisions.

SAP Analytics Cloud Planning provides the planning engine at the centre of this approach. SAP Enterprise Planning extends that foundation with SAP-managed domain content, curated data products, SAP Datasphere, and performance steering capabilities powered by SAP Business Data Cloud. Together, they support a direction towards more continuous, AI-assisted planning and decision-making.

The perspective below brings together AI assistants, agents and powerful performance-sensing-and-steering capabilities. The accompanying illustration indicates a phased roadmap and the innovation at SAP continues.

For planners, the intended shift is from spending most of their time assembling the answer to spending more time challenging assumptions, evaluating trade-offs and steering business performance.

1. Why planning needs to move beyond the calendar

Budgets, quarterly forecasts and monthly performance reviews give organisations structure. But the conditions behind those plans do not wait for the next planning cycle.

Demand changes. Input costs move. Hiring assumptions shift. A customer delays an order. Each event can affect revenue, margin, capacity and cash—but the implications may sit across different teams and planning models.

The challenge is not just to detect a change. It is to connect that change to a decision:

  • What has moved?

  • Why does it matter?

  • Which assumptions need revisiting?

  • What options do we have?

  • Who needs to approve the response?

SAP’s direction addresses this gap through agents that monitor internal and external signals, assess deviations against KPIs and planning assumptions, and help evaluate appropriate responses. Periodic planning remains important; continuous steering adds a way to respond between those cycles.

2. The big picture: a connected planning brain

SAP Analytics Cloud Planning is at the centre of three connected elements:

  1. The planning foundation: models, versions, assumptions, calculations and planning processes.

  2. SAP Planning and Analytics agents: specialised assistance across preparation, modelling, analysis, simulation and communication.

  3. Performance Steeing intelligence: identifying changing conditions and coordinating the planning response.

Joule Work is shown as part of the experience connecting users with this planning environment. The eight-step process beneath the architecture connects the technology to the business lifecycle - from setting targets through forecasting, alignment, performance analysis and executive storytelling.

The “planning brain” is a useful way to describe the relationship between these elements. I am representing this as a planning environment in which data, business logic, analysis and actions become more closely connected. SAP Analytics Cloud Planning is the core planning engine delivering Enterprise-wise Financial and Extended Planning capabilities.

3. Planning and Analytics agents across the planning lifecycle

The agents in the illustration above address different aspects of planning work. The table below summarises their intended contribution at a business level; exact capabilities and availability should be checked against the current roadmap and released documentation as these reach SAP General Availability (GA):

 


Agentic CapabilityIntended contribution to planning processesIndicative  timeline*
Enterprise Planning & Simulation AgentAssist with planning activities and scenario exploration.Q4 2026
Data Action Design AgentAssist with designing the calculation logic used in planning processes.Q4 2026
Analytics & Planning Model Creation AgentAssist with translating analytical and planning requirements into model structures.Q4 2026
Data & Analytics Insights AgentSupport the creation of data-driven analytical experiences and insights.Q4 2026
Analytics Narrative AgentHelp turn analytical findings into understandable business narratives.Q4 2026
Plan Data Upload AgentAssist with bringing planning inputs into the planning environment.Q1 2027
*These are roadmap indications, not confirmation of general availability.
 

The distinction between the agents matters. Creating a model is different from designing its calculations. Producing an analytical insight is different from explaining its implications to the CFO's organisation. Preparing a scenario is different from deciding whether the business should adopt it.

The value comes from connecting these activities while keeping their purposes and the associated review responsibilities clear.

The upper layer in my illustration extends the perspective beyond individual planning tasks with a focus on steering with a wider enterprise performance management lens. Further details on this can be found here.

4. What this means across the enterprise planning process

In my illustration, I show eight stages of planning as a typical examaple. Rather than assigning one agent rigidly to each stage, it is more useful to consider the business outcome each stage needs to support.

 
Planning stages where agent-supported work could help bring transformation capabilities to the planner:
Strategise and set targetsBring relevant trends, assumptions and performance context into target discussions.
Predict baselines, collaborate and adjustEstablish starting forecasts and help contributors explore changes to assumptions.
Data validation and controlsHelp prepare inputs and identify issues for review, without replacing validation rules or accountability.
Predictive and scenario modellingExplore alternatives and compare their financial and operational implications.
Budget and plan approval, continuous forecastingPrepare proposed updates and supporting analysis for authorised review.
Consolidate and alignSupport alignment across planning contributions, assumptions and calculations.
Performance analytics and reportingInvestigate deviations and focus attention on material changes.
Executive storytellingTranslate findings into audience-appropriate explanations and decision points.

The above is my illustrative of potential business mapping, not an official assignment of agent capabilities.

Here, “consolidate and align” means bringing planning contributions together in a planning process. Important to note that when this focus on Financial Consolidation in a Statutory, Managerial and Planning context, we have some great updates coming as part of the SAP Enterprise Performance Management Strategy coming up in 2027. 

5. From FP&A to Enterprise Wide Planning: the same decision, viewed across functions

Consider a life sciences enterprise facing softer demand and higher material costs.

From an FP&A perspective, the immediate questions concern revenue, margin, expenditure and cash. But when looking further as an extended enterprise planning perspective, answering those questions requires connected assumptions from sales, procurement, production and workforce planning.

In this new agentic world, an agent-supported workflow could shorten the path from detecting a change to evaluating and approving a response:

>Detect and investigate

A material deviation prompts investigation. Finance and business owners assess whether the change reflects volume, price, mix, timing or cost pressure.

Market context can inform the analysis, but it should not be mistaken for proof of the underlying cause.

>Evaluate alternatives

The team compares responses: adjust production, revise purchasing assumptions, change commercial activity or defer discretionary expenditure.

The objective is not simply another forecast version. It is an understandable comparison of the trade-offs.

>Review and approve

Decision-makers challenge the assumptions, assess uncertainty and agree the response. Authorised users approve the relevant planning changes.

>Explain the outcome

The resulting narrative connects the signal, the financial implications, the options considered and the decision taken.

This scenario illustrates SAP’s broader direction: connecting signals, impact assessment, scenario evaluation and planning actions while maintaining human oversight. It is not a claim that every step is available today as one end-to-end workflow.

6. How the planner’s work changes

The intended transformation is a redistribution of effort, not the removal of planning expertise. Now lets map the traditional planning apporach to embracing Agentic workflows in planning:

Collecting and preparing inputsReviewing input quality, exceptions and business relevance
Building models and calculation logic manuallyDefining requirements and validating generated structures and logic
Searching through reports for issuesInvestigating prioritised deviations and signals
Rebuilding scenariosChallenging assumptions and comparing alternatives
Writing commentary from a blank pageReviewing, refining and contextualising draft explanations
Coordinating disconnected tasksGoverning a more connected decision process

The planner’s role shifts further towards decision support and performance steering, with less time spent assembling the underlying analysis. They will not just be the curator of AI-generated outputs. In my experience, the greatest value comes when finance can spend more time challenging assumptions and shaping the response, not simply explaining the numbers.

It requires financial judgement, operational understanding and the confidence to reject a plausible recommendation when its assumptions do not hold. We NEED to retain that very important human oversight as part of the planning experience.

7. Building on the planning and analytics foundation

Agents should not be presented within the organisation as replacing the capabilities already supporting planning teams.

Models, calculations, forecasting methods, versions, analytics and workflows remain the foundation. SAP Enterprise Planning combines these planning capabilities with natural-language queries, AI-assisted insights and an agentic layer for steering like never before.

A useful distinction is:

  • Analytical and predictive capabilities provide evidence, forecasts and simulations.

  • Assistance helps my planners interact with those capabilities.

  • Agentic workflows coordinate multiple activities around a business objective.

Do you have a strong foundation? This is why the quality of the underlying planning environment matters. Faster execution of an unclear calculation or an inconsistent business definition does not produce a better decision.

8. Trust and governance belong in the design

As assistance extends into planning actions, the questions become more consequential.

Who can create or change a model? Which users can run calculations? Can an agent prepare a proposed update but not publish it? Which actions require approval? How will a reviewer understand the assumptions behind a recommendation?

SAP describes its enterprise planning approach as using governed data products, controlled planning models, access controls and auditable planning outcomes. Those principles still need to be translated into the configuration and operating model of each implementation.

For an initial use case, define:

  • The permitted actions and data access.

  • The assumptions and outputs that require review.

  • The approval boundary before changes become effective.

  • The evidence needed to explain a recommendation.

  • The process for correcting or rejecting an unsuitable result.

Automation and accountability need to develop together.

9. Roadmap and practical preparation

The illustration indicates a phased direction as SAP continues to innovate rapidly in the Enterprise Planning space. It is important for each organisation to be prepared on how to deliver to the business:

A practical preparation sequence could be as follows:

  1. Select a decision-focused use case. For example start with rolling-forecast preparation, scenario evaluation or variance commentary - not just focusing on deploy agents as an objective.

  2. Review the foundation. Check model structures, business definitions, input quality and calculation logic.

  3. Establish approval boundaries. Separate assistance, proposed changes and authorised execution.

  4. Confirm availability and entitlements. Validate release status, prerequisites, licensing and applicable AI consumption requirements.

  5. Measure business value. Track preparation time, scenario turnaround, review effort and decision quality.

As always, roadmap information is forward-looking and subject to change. Use released documentation to confirm functionality and availability.

A Closing perspective

Planning agents offer a way to connect work that has often been fragmented: preparing the model, understanding a deviation, testing a response and explaining a decision.

For FP&A, that creates the potential for more timely financial insight. For Extended and Enterprise-wide planning, it creates the potential to connect that insight with the operational assumptions and actions behind it.

The question is not how much of the planning cycle can be handed to an agent. It is where assistance can improve the quality and speed of a business decision and where human judgement must remain explicit.

Which part of your planning cycle would benefit most from that change, and where would you retain a mandatory human approval?

entry.title: Joule Agents on SAP Cloud ERP Private: What Really Happens When You Try to Activate One
entry.content:
There are three ways to get a Joule agent working on SAP Cloud ERP Private. Before any of them matters, there is one check that decides whether a single one of them is open to you.

You have AI Units on the contract. Business Data Cloud is provisioned. Finance has an approved use case and a sponsor.

Someone asks you the obvious question: "We have S/4HANA, Business Data Cloud and AI Units. So which agents do we build in S/4, and which ones on BDC?"

It is a good question from a well prepared team, and it contains a category error. Neither S/4HANA nor Business Data Cloud is a place where agents are built. But that is not the reason the project stalls. You open the agent's Discovery Center page, and the minimum release is SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01, restricted to Early Adopter Care. Production is on 2023. Today the answer is not one platform or the other. It is none of the three paths, and nobody in the conversation had mentioned it.

There is also something that has to be settled before any of that, and it is not one of the three paths.

It is the release. On SAP Cloud ERP Private the minimum release differs per agent. The Accounting Accruals Agent used in this example requires S/4HANA 2025 FPS01, and at the time of writing it is available only to customers enrolled in Early Adopter Care. Check each agent against SAP Note 3789370 rather than assuming a common floor.

Once a landscape is above that line, two things decide which path applies: what the thing has to produce when it finishes, and how far it has to reach to produce it. Answer those and the path picks itself.

So this post does two things. It establishes where to check that first, and then it walks the three paths that the choice is actually between, with one finance process carried along each of them.

Reach drawn as radius. Each path stops at a boundary, and that boundary is the reason the next one exists.

Three words worth getting right

Most of the confusion in these conversations is vocabulary, not architecture.

Term

What it actually is

Joule Assistant

The orchestrator. It takes the user's intent, plans the work, picks which agents to invoke, sequences them, and assembles the answer. It decides the what and the when.

Joule Agent

A task executor with a narrow, pre-defined scope. It decides how to accomplish its objective inside that scope. It does not control the wider flow.

Agent Extension

A Joule Studio solution type. SAP's own description: custom skills, instructions or data fields added to existing SAP agents.

The last one is the one most people have never heard of, and it is the one that resolves the majority of these conversations.

And a second set, because SAP renamed the products

In 2025 SAP renamed its cloud ERP offerings, and the rename is still visible in some places and not others. The old and new names both circulate.

  • SAP Cloud ERP was S/4HANA Cloud, public edition. Multi-tenant, SAP schedules the upgrades, no deferral, standard code cannot be modified. The journey is SAP GROW.
  • SAP Cloud ERP Private was S/4HANA Cloud, private edition. Single tenant, the customer schedules upgrades and can defer them, full ABAP development. The journey is RISE with SAP.
  • SAP HANA Cloud is not ERP at all. It is a managed database service on BTP, and it is what Datasphere and Business Data Cloud sit on. Every S/4HANA system uses a HANA database internally, but that is not the product. A customer who says "we are on HANA Cloud" has told you about their data platform and nothing about their ERP.

That confusion matters more than it looks. Before you can compare paths you need to know which ERP edition the customer runs, because the edition decides which agents exist for them at all. The same agent can be available on one edition and absent on the other, so an answer about their data platform does not answer the question you asked.

Path one: activate what SAP already delivers

The test for this path is simple. Does SAP's encoded logic already match how the customer works? If it does, nothing gets built.

Take the SAP Accounting Accruals Agent, reached through the Financial Closing Assistant, as the worked example. Here is what actually happens.

An accountant asks in Joule to prepare accruals for a period and company code. The Assistant routes the intent to the agent. The agent reads two things: the company's own accrual policy handbook, uploaded as a document, and transaction data in the Universal Journal, which includes open purchase orders, goods receipts without an invoice, prepayments and the GR/IR clearing account, plus what is already posted for the period so it does not duplicate. It applies the policy rules against a configured materiality threshold, and produces journal entry proposals, each one carrying a plain-language rationale naming the transactions and the rule it applied.

Those proposals land in the Manage Accrual Proposals Fiori app, where a GL accountant accepts, modifies or rejects each one and posts the accepted entries.

The agent does not post. That is the product, not a configuration choice. That single fact answers most of what a finance team wants to know before it lets an agent near the ledger.

Two things about this flow that surprise people

First, a delivered agent is reading the organisation's own document. If you assume that an SAP-delivered agent cannot read your own documents, you will start building a custom agent when uploading a file would have been enough. That single assumption is the most common reason teams reach for Build when Activate would have worked.

The handbook has real constraints worth knowing before you promise anything. It is uploaded by asking Joule for it from the Manage Accrual Proposals app. It must be a PDF, it supports a maximum of five expense categories before proposal generation times out, and it must name company codes, expense categories and calculation rules, with everything for a given company code in one document. A new upload overwrites the previous one immediately, with no versioning and no approval workflow, which is worth knowing before a period close depends on it.

Second, the minimum release is per agent, not per product. On SAP Cloud ERP Private the Autonomous Finance agents currently require S/4HANA 2025 FPS01. The SAP Discovery Center pages for the Accounting Accruals Agent and the Receivables and Payables Clearing Agent both state that version, and both list the agent as available only to customers enrolled in an Early Adopter Care programme. SAP Note 3789370 carries the same picture for Private Edition. Check the agent's own page against the system's release rather than relying on a product-level answer.

Activation is not a project. It is three things: switching the agent on, writing the policy document it reads, and training the people who work the review app. You know it worked when the team closes one period with the agent running beside them. If that is all the customer needs, stop here. There is no reason to look at the other two paths.

Path two: extend what SAP delivers

The test here is the one that separates most real conversations from imagined ones. Is this the same output, computed by a different rule?

If the customer's process produces the same thing SAP's agent produces but arrives at it differently, you extend. You do not replace.

Agent Extensions are a named solution type in Joule Studio, alongside Agents, n8n Workflows and Applications. SAP's Architecture Center describes what one consists of in a single line: custom skills, instructions or data fields added to existing SAP agents. Three things, named.

Stay with the accruals example. Suppose the business accrues freight from contracted lane rates held in a custom field on the purchase order, while SAP's logic reads invoice history. And suppose the European company codes work to a different materiality threshold from the US ones. Neither of those is a new process. Both still end in an accrual proposal, reviewed in the
same app and posted to the same ledger. That is the test for Extend rather than Build: the thing the agent produces does not change, only the rule that produces it. Three changes cover it. A custom data field makes the lane rate visible to the calculation.
A custom instruction sets materiality by company code instead of one global number. And a custom skill calls a control the delivered agent does not know about.

What the customer keeps

This is the part most often left out of the comparison.

  • SAP's data reads stay as delivered
  • The output is still an accrual proposal, carrying its reasoning
  • SAP keeps maintaining and upgrading the delivered agent, so the underlying logic stays their responsibility rather than becoming yours. With a custom agent, that maintenance moves to you.
  • SAP keeps maintaining and upgrading the delivered agent, so the underlying logic stays their responsibility rather than becoming yours. With a custom agent, that maintenance moves to you.

That last point matters more than it looks. Extend, and the agent is positioned to inherit SAP's next version. Rebuild the same thing from scratch and it has to be maintained against every release, which is a cost that shows up in year two rather than year one.

Two honest limits

Extensions do not port between editions. SAP's clean core guidance puts it plainly: extensions created for private edition generally require adaptations to be portable to the public cloud, side-by-side extensions on BTP are more likely to be compatible because they decouple the logic from the core, and complete parity is not guaranteed because API availability and scope differ across editions. There is a second, more practical point at the time of writing. Every published extension tutorial targets a Public Edition agent, and I could not find one that extends a Private Edition agent. Whether that reflects what the catalogue actually offers, or only what has been written up so far, I cannot tell from public sources. Worth checking against your own tenant rather than taking from a post.

And the upgrade behaviour is positioning, not a published guarantee. SAP has built extension as the path that respects the release train, and that is the architectural intent. The mechanism itself is not documented, and extension points appear to be declared per agent rather than universally. Worth confirming for the specific agent rather than assuming it holds generally.

Path three: build in Joule Studio

The test for this one: is the output a different thing entirely?

If what the customer wants does not exist as an SAP business object, no delivered agent will ever produce it, because it is not an SAP process. It is this company's question. That is when you build, and it is the only honest reason to.

Stay with finance and the shape is obvious. The accruals agent produces a proposal. Suppose the CFO wants something else: two weeks before close, what the accrual exposure is likely to land at across the whole group, including commitments sitting in a third-party receivables platform that never enters S/4HANA, compared against the same quarter in prior years that the ERP no longer keeps online.

That is not an accrual proposal. It is a briefing with a recommendation. Different object, so neither activate nor extend can reach it.

What a Joule Studio agent is actually made of

An agent is a definition plus a set of tools, not a programme.

The definition carries a name, a description, its expertise and its instructions, and Joule uses that description to decide when to route a request to it. You select a model available through the generative AI hub. Then you add tools. The assignable tool types today are:

  • Joule Skills, single deterministic actions
  • Actions, API calls to SAP or third-party systems
  • Automations, Build Process Automation workflows
  • Document grounding resource groups
  • MCP server tools, reached over BTP destinations
  • Other custom agents, used as subagents
  • Human-in-the-loop confirmation points, so the agent pauses for approval at the decisions that matter

This is where Business Data Cloud genuinely belongs, and notice that it arrived on the third path rather than the first. A question that spans entities, spans years and spans systems is exactly what the data layer exists for, and almost nothing before this point needed it.

One limit people assume away

A custom agent can use other custom agents as subagents. It cannot call an SAP-delivered agent. The current interoperability model works inbound: a third-party or custom agent can invoke a delivered Joule Agent through the Agent Gateway. The reverse, a Joule Studio agent calling a delivered SAP agent, is a later iteration, and Joule orchestrating mixed chains of delivered and custom agents is planned rather than shipped.

So a design that assumes a new agent will delegate to the Accruals Agent needs checking before it reaches a whiteboard.

One more thing worth stating plainly, because it is the first question anyone responsible for the ledger will ask: a custom agent runs in the calling user's security context. SAP's own product page puts it directly, saying that all agent traffic flows through the agent gateway, so agents can only execute what the end user has permission to do directly. An agent is not a route around access control.

 

One front door, three places the work lands, and only the third reaching outside the ERP.

The boundary nobody checks

Everything above is about choosing a path. This section is about whether the customer's use case is reachable from any of them, and it is the part most often skipped.

An agent activation is scoped to one backend and one client.

The mechanism is the skills mapping. Each agent has pre-defined Joule Skills that map to specific intended back ends, and only back ends with official, delivered skills are eligible targets for that agent's execution. Routing follows the step ownership defined in the delivered process. There is no mechanism for a single active agent to query or route across multiple clients or backend systems within one conversation turn.

Joule can surface agents from different connected systems in the same interface, which is why this is easy to miss. But each agent still executes against the backend its skills were mapped to, and SAP's product page states the permission boundary directly: all agent traffic flows through the agent gateway, so agents can only execute what the end user has permission to do directly.

How many systems one Joule instance can front is a separate question, and SAP's documentation currently disagrees with itself about it. The constraints pages say a Joule instance links to a single S/4HANA system. The Q2 2026 release notes and the Joule Feature Summary Document say Joule supports connecting multiple Private Edition and Public Edition systems within one formation. Until those reconcile it is not a number worth quoting. What holds either way is the agent-level constraint above: whatever Joule can front, an individual agent still executes against one backend.

Why this decides so many conversations

Consider a landscape with one production client live today and further regional clients built and tested but not yet promoted. Everything works. The agent sits in the live client, reads what it needs, proposes, a person posts.

Now the regional waves land. Each client that goes live needs its own activation, and each of those agents executes against its own client. Joule can front all of them, so a user still asks one question and is routed to the right system. What no single agent does is reason across all five in one turn.

One activation per client. Joule fronts all of them; no single agent reasons across them.

So the question that genuinely spans the clients is not answered by any delivered agent, and it is not answered by an extension either, because extending changes the rule and not the reach. It is answerable where those clients converge, which is the data layer. That is the honest case for Business Data Cloud, and it is a better case than the one usually made for it, because it comes from a constraint rather than from a product sheet.

This belongs alongside the release check, before the catalogue is opened at all. A use case whose data sits in another client, another instance, or in a legacy ERP that only replicates financial documents in, is not reachable from the activate path however many AI Units are already paid for.

What this looks like in a real landscape

A worked example makes this concrete. What follows is a real customer environment with the identifying detail stripped out. Nothing in it is unusual, and that is exactly why it is worth walking through.

They run Cloud ERP Private on release 2023, with a second landscape on release 2025 being built in parallel. Production carries one business client. Several further clients exist in quality and development, configured and tested, waiting on the regional rollout. Central Finance is live, replicating financial documents in from legacy ERP systems still running finance in some parts of the world.

Four things follow from that. The first three are checkable; the fourth is a question I could not resolve.

None of the three paths is open to them yet. The finance agents need 2025 FPS01 and Early Adopter Care enrolment, and the business runs on 2023. The second landscape is where the paths become available, so the first move is finishing that migration, not choosing between agents.

This limit is not theoretical, and it already has a date. With one production client today, one activation covers the whole business and nobody runs into a boundary. When the regional clients go live, each one needs its own agent, and no single agent can answer a question that spans them. That is the moment Build becomes the honest answer, and the go-live date for those clients is already in somebody's plan.

Central Finance changes what the agent can see. The accruals agent reads open purchase orders, goods receipts without an invoice, and the GR/IR clearing account. Central Finance replicates financial and controlling postings plus a defined subset of logistics through the accounting view of logistics. That is an accounting view, not the logistics document chain. Whether it satisfies what the agent's logic expects is a real question, and I have not seen it answered publicly. The practical consequence is that processes posted natively in the live client are reachable, and regions still running in a legacy ERP are not.

Almost the whole surrounding stack is already there. Cloud Identity Services, Build Work Zone, the connectivity and destination services, Integration Suite and the Business AI Platform are all live in the production landscape, as are Business Data Cloud and Datasphere. When the release does arrive, this is a configuration exercise rather than a procurement one, which is worth establishing on any landscape early.

Four questions, in order

These work on any process, not only finance, and they take about five minutes.

Which release is it on, and is the agent available there?

The product, the release and the feature pack, then that agent's own Discovery Center page. On Cloud ERP Private the finance agents need 2025 FPS01 and Early Adopter Care enrolment. Below that line there is no path to choose yet, and every question after this one is academic.

What does it produce, and where is the data?

A posted document, a cleared item, a proposal for review, or a briefing. If the output is the same business object SAP's agent already produces, the answer is path one or two. A different object means path three. Then: which client holds the data it needs, because one agent reads one backend and one client.

Is the gap the process, or the rule?

Does SAP's agent do the right job the wrong way, or the wrong job entirely? Right job, wrong way is an extension, and it is usually a few fields and an instruction. Wrong job entirely is the only honest reason to build. This is the question most often skipped, and skipping it is how a few fields and an instruction turn into a project.

Does the non-SAP system supply data, or make decisions?

A non-SAP system is either a source you read from or a system that acts on its own. Reading its data is a connection you configure, which keeps you on the Build path with a shape you can scope and price. Having that system make decisions on your behalf is a different problem, and not all of it is available today. Answering this question tells you whether Build means a data connection you can commit to now, or something you should not promise yet.

Most of these conversations start at Build, because that is the conversation the market has trained everyone to have. Starting at the release and working down is the shorter route to something that actually ships.

* Product behaviour changes quickly here. Everything above is current as of late October 2026, and the per-agent release floors in particular are worth re-checking rather than quoting from a post.

entry.title: Identity Propagation from Joule to SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
During workforce management reviews, HR managers and administrators frequently need to audit employee contract extension data. Searching through nested SAP SuccessFactors menus or manually parsing custom Metadata Framework (MDF) objects introduces friction into routine operations.

By integrating Joule with custom extension agents on SAP BTP, users can query sensitive custom MDF objects—such as Contract Renewal entities—using natural language while dynamically enforcing SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP) for every tool call.

Scenario Overview

  • Intent Initiation via Digital Assistant: An HR administrator or standard employee queries Joule using natural language to retrieve or verify contract renewal cases for an employee.
  • Identity Propagation & Session Context: Joule interprets the prompt and executes user identity propagation (principal propagation) down to SAP SuccessFactors, ensuring that the authenticated user's session context is preserved end-to-end.
  • Context-Aware RBP Enforcement: The custom agent fetches data directly from SuccessFactors OData APIs. Access to sensitive fields (such as salary adjustments or contract terms) is governed entirely by the user's assigned SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

This article walks through the end-to-end configuration: setting up trust between Joule and SuccessFactors, enabling principal propagation, and enforcing role-based access to the custom Contract Renewal MDF object.

Prerequisites

To successfully implement this architecture, ensure that the following system dependencies and administrative privileges are in place:

  • SAP BTP Subaccount with Joule Enabled: An active subaccount on SAP BTP with the Joule digital assistant entitlement subscribed and provisioned.
  • SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS): An IAS tenant configured as the Identity Provider for both your SAP BTP subaccount and your SAP SuccessFactors instance to enable OpenID Connect (OIDC) and SAML token exchanges.
  • Custom MDF Object in SuccessFactors: A custom Metadata Framework (MDF) object—such as Contract Renewal—created via Configure Object Definitions in SuccessFactors.
  • Role-Based Permissions (RBP) Configured: Specific permissions assigned in SuccessFactors RBP for the custom MDF object (e.g., read/write access granted to HR Manager, and restricted for Standard User).
  • Administrative Access: Administrator privileges across the SAP BTP Cockpit, the SAP IAS Administration Console, and the SuccessFactors Admin Center.
  • Protocol Familiarity: Basic understanding of OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect (OIDC), JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SAML 2.0 bearer assertions.

Architecture Overview

The following diagram illustrates the end-to-end trust chain and identity flow between Joule, SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Identity Services, and SAP SuccessFactors:
 
The identity flow begins when a user authenticates in Joule via SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS). Joule’s A2A client routes the prompt through a BTP Destination to the pro-code custom agent on SAP Cloud Foundry. The agent validates and forwards the user token, using a second BTP Destination to execute a SAML Bearer Assertion against SAP SuccessFactors. This ensures the request hits the OData API Center with the user's active session context, dynamically enforcing Role-Based Permissions (RBP) at the backend metadata layer.
 

Generate the SAML Signing Certificate

The BTP Destination Service will sign SAML assertions using a certificate. SuccessFactors needs that certificate registered to trust those assertions. Two commands are needed here because the outputs serve two different purposes and go to two different systems.

The first command generates the raw key material in PEM format — certificate.pem  is the public certificate you upload to SuccessFactors, and privateKey.pem is the private key that stays on your machine.

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 3650 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/certificate.pem \
  -subj "/CN=sfsf-assistant-saml"

The second command takes those two PEM files and bundles them together into a PKCS#12 keystore (.p12). This is the format BTP Destination Service expects when it needs to sign SAML assertions on behalf of your application — a plain PEM file is not sufficient for this purpose.

openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -in certs/certificate.pem \
  -inkey certs/privateKey.pem \
  -out certs/sfsf-saml-client.p12 \
  -name "sfsf-saml-client" \
  -password pass:yourpassword

certificate.pem goes to SuccessFactors when registering the OAuth2 client. sfsf-saml-client.p12 goes to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. Remember, the password for your .p12 certificate will be required when you use it in the destination configuration. 

Register an OAuth2 Client in SuccessFactors

SuccessFactors needs to know your app's signing certificate before it will accept SAML assertions from it.

1. Log in to SuccessFactors Admin Center. Navigate to Admin Center → Manage OAuth2 Client Applications or Under the tools Search field type Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and click the link in the search results.

2. Click Register Client Application

3. When you click Register Client Application under Manage OAuth2 Client Applications in SAP SuccessFactors, you will need to fill out the following form fields:

  • Company: Pre-filled automatically based on your current SuccessFactors instance or tenant ID.
  • Application Name: A unique, descriptive name for your client application or integration.
  • Description (Optional): A short note explaining the purpose of the application or integration.
  • Application URL: A valid URL pointing to the client application or vendor's website domain.
  • X.509 Certificate: Paste your pre-generated public certificate text which we generated in the previous section.

and click Register

4. After clicking Register, the system generates a public API Key required for authenticating your API requests. To retrieve this key, locate your new client entry in the list, navigate to the Actions column, and click View.

5.Locate the generated API Key. Copy it and store it safely, as your external application will require it to complete the connection.

Maintain the Generated Certificate in BTP Destination Service

Before configuring the destination itself, the .p12 keystore must be uploaded to the BTP Destination Service certificate store. The destination references it by name — it is never embedded inline.

1. Login into the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your Subaccount. Go to Connectivity and navigate directly to Destination Certificates and click on Import Button.

2. Click the Upload button to select your certificate file from your local file system

3. Select sfsf-saml-client.p12  from your local machine and click on Open button.

4. Click on Create button

Once uploaded, the certificate appears in the list with the name sfsf-saml-client.p12. This is the exact value you will enter as Key Store Location when configuring the sfsf-conn destination.

The certificate store is scoped to your BTP subaccount. Multiple destinations in the same subaccount can reference the same uploaded keystore.

Import the Destinations

With the certificate uploaded, you can now create the destination that performs the actual principal propagation. This destination is what your application calls to exchange the user's IAS token for a SuccessFactors OAuth token.
Rather than filling in every property manually, download the pre-built destination file below and import it directly into BTP. You only need to update the four placeholder values specific to your SuccessFactors tenant before importing.

Download: (destinations/sfsf-conn.properties)

Open the file and replace the following placeholders with your own values:

Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
KeyStoreLocation=sfsf-saml-client.p12
KeyStorePassword=<keystore-password>
Name=sfsf-conn
ProxyType=Internet
SAMLAssertionProvider=DestinationServiceGenerated
Type=HTTP
URL=<successfactors-api-url>
apiKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
audience=www.successfactors.com
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession
clientKey=<generated-api-key-in-successfactor>
companyId=<company-id-in-successfactor>
includeSigningCertificateInSAMLAssertion=true
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:unspecified
skipUserAttributesPrefixInSAMLAttributes=true
skipUserUuidInSAMLAttributes=true
tokenServiceURL=<successfactors-api-url>/oauth/token
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
  • <successfactors-api-url>:  SAP  API domain (e.g., api12sales.successfactors.eu) — appears in both URL and tokenServiceURL
  • <generated-api-key-in-successfactor>: The API Key (Client ID) generated during OAuth2 registration in SF — appears in both clientKey and apiKey.
  • <company-id-in-successfactor>:  Your SAP SF company/tenant ID.
  • <keystore-password>:  The password set for the uploaded .p12 X.509 certificate used for SAML signing.

All other properties — authentication type, SAML settings, certificate flags — are already correctly configured in the file. Once you have updated the placeholders, import the file into BTP:

1. Go to BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations then click Create.

2. In the Create New Destination dialog box, select From File to import an already configured destination.

3. Select sfsf-conn.properties from your local machine, then click Open.

4. Destination successfully imported, Click OK.

5. On the destination detail page, click Check Connection. A successful Check Connection confirms the destination is correctly configured and reachable.

Principal Propagation from Joule to Agent

With Joule’s Pro-Code Extensibility, customers can seamlessly integrate custom, code-based agents into the Joule ecosystem using third-party frameworks—a paradigm known as "Bring Your Own Agent" (BYOA). Rather than relying solely on declarative Joule frameworks, a BYOA agent operates as a standard, code-based application that communicates directly with Joule via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. However, extending Joule’s capabilities with custom logic requires careful consideration of how enterprise data is accessed.

For any production-grade agent interacting with core enterprise platforms like SAP SuccessFactors, implementing Principal Propagation (User Identity Propagation) is non-negotiable. Omitting identity propagation forces the agent to execute requests under a generic technical user identity, which inherently bypasses individual Role-Based Permissions (RBP) and exposes the organization to major architectural, security, and governance risks.

With principal propagation active, data authorization is enforced directly at the backend source system layer in SuccessFactors. This guarantees that unauthorized data payloads are stopped at the source and never exposed to intermediate agent layers or the client application — making identity propagation the core mechanism for maintaining strict enterprise compliance.

Achieving this level of security requires building a continuous chain of trust across the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). The previous steps established the connection between SAP SuccessFactors and the BTP environment to enable user-propagated API calls. The next phase establishes trust between Joule and the agent. The resulting end-to-end authentication pipeline flows from the Joule-managed SAP Identity Authentication Service (IAS) tenant, through the agent, and directly into SAP SuccessFactors — yielding a stateless, credential-less agent that holds no long-lived backend credentials, ensuring every backend request is executed strictly within the real-time permissions of the logged-in user.

The setup for establishing trust between Joule and the agent follows the foundation outlined by Felix Bartler in his article, Joule A2A: Propagate the User Identity from Joule into S/4HANA. You may follow the steps directly from Felix's guide or proceed with the tailored implementation steps outlined below.

Registering the IAS Applications for App-to-App Trust

IAS acts as the gatekeeper for every token exchange in this chain. Before Joule can hand its token to your agent, IAS needs to know who each participant is and needs explicit authorization for each step in the exchange. That means registering two OpenID Connect applications — one representing the proxy, one representing your agent — and then drawing the permission path between them.

Both applications must be created in the same IAS tenant where your BTP subaccount established trust during Joule provisioning. You can confirm which tenant that is under Subaccount → Security → Trust Configuration.

Create the IAS Applications

In the IAS admin panel, navigate to Applications & Resources → Applications and create two OpenID Connect applications:

1. A2A_Proxy_App — the intermediary that receives Joule's token and hands it forward. After creating it, expose an API resource on the application (e.g., a2a_proxy_app_api). This API defines the audience (aud) claim that exchanged tokens will carry, which IAS uses to validate that the exchange is directed at the right target.

2. A2A_Custom_Agent_Apps — the application representing your actual agent, the one that will call SuccessFactors. Expose an API resource here as well (e.g., a2a_custom_agent_app_api), for the same reason.

Configure the Trust Chain

Dependencies in IAS define which token exchanges are permitted. In this setup, you need to configure two specific application dependencies: the inbound Joule proxy dependency and the downstream target application dependency.

1. Joule → Proxy: Locate the pre-existing Joule IAS application in your tenant. Add a dependency targeting A2A_Proxy_App  and select its exposed API. Name this dependency exactly joule-to-proxy — this string is hardcoded into Joule's runtime and cannot be changed.

2. Proxy → Agent: Open A2A_Proxy_App and add a dependency targeting  A2A_Custom_Agent_App. Name it proxy-to-target. This name is your choice, but you will need to reference it exactly in the BTP Destination configuration in the next section.

Because the joule-to-proxy dependency is fixed to your proxy app once, adding a future agent requires only a new IAS application and a new proxy-to-<name> dependency on the same proxy — no changes to Joule's configuration.

Finally, generate a client secret on A2A_Proxy_App under Client Authentication → Secrets. The BTP Destination Service will use these credentials to authenticate as the proxy when performing the second token exchange. Save the client ID and secret — you will need them in the next section.

Bring Your Own Agent (BYOA) and Extend Joule Capabilities

To simplify building pro-code custom agents for Joule, we leverage the SAP A2A Agent Toolkit — a skill for Claude Code that scaffolds a complete pro-code agent alongside a Joule capability and Cloud Foundry deployment config in a single command. Supporting both Python and TypeScript, it seamlessly integrates with LangGraph and SAP AI Core / GenAI Hub, handling everything from agent creation to A2A protocol wiring and Joule registration. You can explore the skill page and find the source code in the GitHub repository.

For this SAP SuccessFactors scenario, you can build the agent and Joule capability from scratch using the toolkit—or take the faster path by cloning this ready-to-use reference template from GitHub, which comes with principal propagation pre-configured. With just a few environment updates, your agent and Joule capability will be ready for deployment.

git clone https://github.com/alphageek7443/sfsf-assistant.git
cd sfsf-assistant

The project structure includes exactly what the toolkit generates:

  • app/ — Core agent implementation and business logic.
  • joule-capability/ — Joule capability definitions and A2A wiring.
  • manifest.yml —Cloud Foundry deployment specification.

Before deploying, let's update the environment placeholders and configuration properties to match your target BTP and SuccessFactors landscapes.

Updating the Cloud Foundry Manifest

The repository comes pre-configured with a manifest.yml structure matching the output of the SAP A2A Agent Toolkit. Open manifest.yml and adjust the environment variables and service bindings to align with your landscape:

applications:
  - name: sfsf-assistant
    memory: 512M
    disk_quota: 1G
    instances: 1
    buildpacks:
      - python_buildpack
    command: python -m app
    env:
      MODEL_NAME: gpt-4.1
      AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP: default
      IAS_ISSUER: https://your-ias-tenant.accounts.ondemand.com
      IAS_AUDIENCE: your-ias-audience-uuid
    services:
      - your-destination-service
    routes:
      - route: your-app.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com

Key Configuration Placeholders to Update:

  • MODEL_NAME & AICORE_RESOURCE_GROUP: Set these to match your active model deployment name and resource group in SAP AI Core / GenAI Hub (e.g., gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, etc.). Ensure your AI Core service binding or secret is configured in BTP to grant access to this model.
  • IAS_ISSUER: Your IAS tenant URL (e.g., https://.accounts.ondemand.com). This must match the exact IAS tenant where you registered the trust and applications earlier.
  • IAS_AUDIENCE: The Client ID of the A2A_Custom_Agent_App (not the proxy app). This is a critical link back to your IAS setup: the agent middleware uses this value to cryptographically verify that inbound user tokens exchanged by Joule are intended for this specific agent.
  • services: Replace your-destination-service with the actual name of your SAP BTP Destination Service instance bound to your subaccount.
  • routes: Update your-app.cfapps..hana.ondemand.com to match your BTP Cloud Foundry region and confirm the route host is unique within your organization.

Deploying the Custom Agent

Provision the Destination Service instance (if not already created) and push the application to Cloud Foundry:

# Create the destination service instance
cf create-service destination lite sfsf-assistant-dest

# Deploy the custom agent
cf push

Once deployed, take note of your application’s live route URL—we will use it later when configuring the BTP HTTP destination to the custom agent.

Key Implementation Patterns

Three core components in the agent application work together to pass the user's identity from the inbound A2A request all the way into SAP SuccessFactors. The agent logic itself (agent.py) remains completely decoupled from security tokens, while two supporting layers handle identity capture and downstream token exchange.

1. Inbound Identity Capture (main.py)

A Starlette middleware intercepts inbound A2A requests, extracts the bearer token, and validates it against your IAS tenant before storing it in the request context:

class IASAuthMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        auth = request.headers.get("authorization", "")
        token = auth.removeprefix("Bearer ").strip() if auth.startswith("Bearer ") else None

        if token and (claims := _verify_ias_token(token)):
            set_user_token(token)  # Store token in context for active request thread

        return await call_next(request)

During local development, setting IAS_ISSUER and IAS_AUDIENCE to local placeholders bypasses token signature checks so you can test using mock tokens without modifying code.

2. Downstream Token Exchange (sfsf_client.py)

When tools fetch data from SuccessFactors, sfsf_client.py retrieves the context token and passes it to the SAP BTP Destination Service via the X-user-token header:

def get_sfsf_token_and_url() -> tuple[str, str]:
    creds = _get_dest_service_creds()
    user_token = get_user_token()

    # Get Destination Service access token
    ds_token = httpx.post(
        f"{creds['url']}/oauth/token",
        data={"grant_type": "client_credentials"},
        auth=(creds["clientid"], creds["clientsecret"]),
    ).json()["access_token"]

    # Request SuccessFactors token with user identity attached
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {ds_token}"}
    if user_token:
        headers["X-user-token"] = user_token  # Triggers SAML assertion for end-user

    dest = httpx.get(
        f"{creds['uri']}/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/sfsf-conn",
        headers=headers,
    ).json()

    return dest["authTokens"][0]["value"], dest["destinationConfiguration"]["URL"].rstrip("/")

Why X-user-token matters: Supplying the X-user-token header instructs the Destination Service to generate a user-bound SAML assertion. If omitted, the service falls back to the technical user configured on the destination, bypassing SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP).

Agent Tool Decoupling (agent.py)

Because the middleware and HTTP client manage identity propagation transparently, tools invoke standard OData calls directly:

@tool
def get_contract_renewal_cases(
    employee_id: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None,
    department: str | None = None,
    faculty: str | None = None,
    top: int = 5,
) -> dict:
    """Fetch contract renewal cases from SuccessFactors.

    Use this tool to look up employment contract renewals, renewal dates, salary
    adjustments, performance grades, approval/review workflow status, and case notes
    for employees. Also covers vendor agreements and internal service transfers.

    Args:
        employee_id: Filter by employee userId (e.g. '103266'). Use userId, not username — resolve via search_employees first if needed.
        status:      Filter by case status (e.g. 'READY_FOR_SS_REVIEW', 'SS_REVIEWED_APPROVED', 'HRP_VALIDATED')
        department:  Filter by department code (e.g. 'ME')
        faculty:     Filter by faculty code (e.g. 'FoE')
        top:         Maximum number of results to return (default 5)
    """
    filters = []
    if employee_id:
        filters.append(f"cust_Employee eq '{employee_id}'")
    if status:
        filters.append(f"cust_status eq '{status}'")
    if department:
        filters.append(f"cust_department eq '{department}'")
    if faculty:
        filters.append(f"cust_faculty eq '{faculty}'")

    params = {
        "$select": (
            "externalCode,externalName,cust_Employee,cust_department,cust_faculty,"
            "cust_designation,cust_currentSalary,cust_newSalary,cust_salaryAdjustment,"
            "cust_performanceGrade,cust_currentEndDate,cust_proposedEndDate,"
            "cust_durationMonths,cust_discussionDate,cust_status,cust_notes,"
            "lastModifiedDateTime,lastModifiedBy,createdDateTime,createdBy"
        ),
        "$orderby": "lastModifiedDateTime desc",
        "$top": str(top),
    }
    if filters:
        params["$filter"] = " and ".join(filters)

    result = sfsf_get("/odata/v2/cust_ContractRenewalCaseV2", params)

    if isinstance(result, dict) and not result.get("error"):
        records = result.get("d", {}).get("results", [])
        if not records:
            return {
                "message": "No contract renewal cases found",
                "filters_applied": {
                    "employee_id": employee_id,
                    "status": status,
                    "department": department,
                    "faculty": faculty,
                },
            }

    return result

Configure and Deploy the Joule Capability

Open joule-capability/capability.sapdas.yaml. The system_aliases block maps a logical name to a BTP destination. The destination name here must exactly match the name of the BTP destination you will create in the next section to point Joule at your agent:

system_aliases:
  SfsfAssistant:
    destination: sfsf-assistant-auth

Leave it as sfsf-assistant-auth unless you plan to use a different destination name—just make sure they match. Next, navigate to the capability directory, authenticate, and deploy the capability to Joule:

Register the Joule Capability

With the agent running, register the capability with Joule:

cd joule-capability
joule deploy -c ./da.sapdas.yaml -n sfsf_assistant_a2a

This compiles and publishes the capability to your Joule tenant. Once the BTP destination is in place, Joule will be able to route user prompts directly to your custom agent.

Configuring the BTP HTTP Destination (Joule -> Custom Agent)

To execute the downstream authentication flow, construct an HTTP destination in your SAP BTP subaccount using the OAuth2JWTBearer authentication type. This destination incorporates specific properties that instruct the SAP BTP Destination Service to execute the token exchange.

Rather than filling in every property manually, download the pre-built destination file below and import it directly into BTP. You only need to update the placeholder values.

Download: (destinations/sfsf-assistant-auth.properties)

Open the file and replace the following placeholders with your own values:

Destination Configuration Parameters

Configure the destination with the following properties:

Name=sfsf-assistant-auth
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2JWTBearer
URL=<your-agent-route>
clientId=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>
clientSecret=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-secret>
tokenServiceURL=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/token
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
apptoapp=true
tokenService.body.token_format=jwt
tokenService.body.client_id=<A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>
tokenService.body.resource=urn:sap:identity:application:provider:name:proxy-to-target
tokenService.addClientCredentialsInBody=false
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs

Four placeholders to fill in:

  • <your-agent-route>:  The Cloud Foundry route URL of your deployed custom agent.
  • <A2A_Proxy_App-client-id>: The Client ID generated for A2A_Proxy_App in IAS -- appears in clientId and tokenService.body.client_id
  • <A2A_Proxy_App-client-secret>:  The Client secret generated for A2A_Proxy_App in IAS
  • <your-ias-tenant>:  Your IAS tenant domain -- appears in tokenServiceURL and x_user_token.jwks_uri

Note: The Name property must exactly match the destination referenced in capability.sapdas.yaml (sfsf-assistant-auth). If you customized the destination alias in your capability file, ensure it matches here character-for-character.

Key Architectural Highlights & Considerations

Proxy Client Credentials: The clientId and clientSecret parameters correspond to the IAS proxy application (A2A_Proxy_App), not the custom agent itself. This destination handles the token assertion request sent to the custom agent. Joule automatically manages the initial authentication flow before resolving this destination.

Dependency Mapping (tokenService.body.resource): This property targets the IAS dependency name. The prefix urn:sap:identity:application:provider:name: must be prepended to the exact target application dependency configured in IAS (e.g., proxy-to-target).

User Token Validation (x_user_token.jwks_uri): This parameter points to the JWKS endpoint of your IAS tenant, enabling the SAP BTP Destination Service to cryptographically validate the inbound end-user token before issuing the downstream assertion. Warning: Omitting x_user_token.jwks_uri causes the Destination Service to fail user token validation and silently fall back to a technical service user, breaking end-to-end principal propagation.

App-to-App Mode (apptoapp=true): Explicitly enables App2App authentication mode within the SAP BTP Destination Service.

End-to-End Execution Flow & Testing

To verify that principal propagation and capability routing function correctly across the entire integration, we test the end-to-end flow in Joule using two distinct user personas with contrasting SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP).

Multi-Persona Verification Highlights

HR Manager Persona (Tessa Walker): When logged in as HR Manager Tessa Walker, the custom agent leverages full authorized access to sensitive employee compensation and contract data:

Broad Query & Disambiguation: Tessa prompts Joule to show contract renewal cases and requests details for a specific employee. The agent detects multiple active employee records associated with the target employee, prompts for clarification, and asks the user to select the target record.

Detailed Record Retrieval: Upon selecting the specific user record, the propagated user identity passes through the BTP Destination service and returns comprehensive contract renewal details, including Case ID, Department, Designation, Faculty, Current Salary, New Salary, Duration, HRP Validation Status, and Performance Grade.

 

Standard User Persona (Benney Cobb): When executing the exact same conversation flow as a standard employee, principal propagation ensures that security boundaries are strictly maintained:

Directory Resolution vs. Restricted Contracts: Benney initiates the same query for the employee. While Benney's RBP correctly permits basic user directory lookups (successfully resolving the employee's name to the matching user IDs), subsequent calls to the sensitive contract entities fail to return records due to a lack of HR management privileges.

Conclusion

Extending Joule with pro-code custom agents via the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol unlocks powerful, enterprise-grade extensibility patterns on SAP BTP. By leveraging Bring Your Own Agent (BYOA) architectures, development teams can build tailored AI agents using tools like LangGraph while maintaining strict security boundaries.

Integrating the SAP BTP Destination Service with App-to-App (App2App) token exchange and X-user-token propagation guarantees that every AI-driven tool call respects SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP). This ensures end-to-end data security, user context preservation, and full auditability without compromising the developer experience.
